Joro proxy-mode confused-deputy: browser POSTs to loopback API 127.0.0.1:9090 (CVE-2026-53649) AIDelivery Low
Hunts a web browser process opening connections to the Joro proxy-mode API on loopback TCP/9090, the confused-deputy vector CVE-2026-53649 abuses when attacker-controlled cross-origin JavaScript reaches the unauthenticated, wildcard-CORS Joro API. Article-specific because it pins the exact bind (127.0.0.1:9090) and the browser-mediated initiator. Rationale: Uses the exact loopback bind (127.0.0.1:9090) named in the advisory plus a browser-process initiator, the confused-deputy shape of CVE-2026-53649. Deliberately hunting/Low because a legitimate Joro operator's own browser talks to the same UI/API port. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling • https://github.com/bishopfox
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Joro operator using the proxy-mode web UI, which itself talks to 127.0.0.1:9090
  • Unrelated local dev services on 9090 (Prometheus Pushgateway, SonarQube, custom app) that a browser hits
  • Browser DevTools/extension polling a localhost dev server on the same port
  • Local reverse-proxy or API mock bound to 9090 during development
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether Joro is installed/running on the host and whether the operator was actively using the Joro UI at that timestamp; pull the browser history for the immediately preceding external navigation. 2) Contain: if the loopback hit was NOT operator-initiated UI use, kill the joro process, isolate the host, and block the external page's domain at the proxy. 3) Hunt: pivot to whether joro subsequently wrote a .so plugin, restarted, or spawned an interactive shell (see companion UCs) — that sequence confirms exploitation.

| where RemotePort == 9090
| where RemoteIP in ("127.0.0.1", "::1")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("firefox","firefox-bin","chrome","chromium","msedge","brave","Google Chrome","Firefox")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc

Joro native plugin RCE: joro process spawns interactive /bin/bash shell (CVE-2026-53649) AIExploitation High
Alerts when the joro binary spawns an interactive Unix shell (bash/sh/dash/zsh with -i), the terminal step of the CVE-2026-53649 chain where a malicious uploaded plugin's init() opens a goroutine and yields an interactive /bin/bash -i shell as the operator's user. High fidelity because joro is a proxy/teamserver, not a shell launcher — it has no legitimate reason to fork a local login shell. Rationale: Pins the article's exact parent (joro) and payload (interactive /bin/bash -i obtained on plugin.Open() init()). Because Joro is a proxy that never legitimately forks a local login shell, parent=joro + shell + -i is a near-zero-FP RCE tell. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.004 T1129
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Joro developer/operator debugging the tool and manually shelling out from a plugin during testing
  • A local wrapper or helper script also named 'joro' that legitimately invokes a shell
  • Operator running a benign self-authored plugin that spawns a shell for tooling
  • CI/build harness building Joro plugins that exec a shell as part of a test
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the child shell's full process tree and any sockets it holds (ss -p); confirm the joro process previously loaded a newly-written .so and restarted. 2) Contain: kill the shell and joro process, isolate the host, and snapshot /proc for the joro PID before termination for the loaded-plugin path. 3) Hunt: enumerate the Joro plugin directory for attacker-uploaded .so files, review recent POSTs to /api/v1/plugins/upload and /api/v1/system/restart, and check outbound connections from joro to external hosts.

| where ProcessCommandLine has "-i"

Joro writes a native .so plugin: attacker plugin drop before restart (CVE-2026-53649) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the joro process writing a shared-object (.so) plugin file to disk, the staging step where CVE-2026-53649's unauthenticated upload endpoint persists an attacker-supplied native plugin that executes its init() on the next plugin.Open(). Article-specific via the joro-process writer plus the .so plugin artifact. Rationale: Ties the article's plugin-upload artifact (a native .so consumed by plugin.Open()) to the joro process as writer. joro dropping a .so it did not build interactively is the on-disk footprint of the upload endpoint being abused. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xqhv-chqm-fhcc • https://bishopfox.com/blog/introducing-joro-using-ai-build-security-tooling
ATT&CKT1129 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator legitimately installing/updating a Joro plugin through the intended workflow
  • Joro's own --build-plugin feature emitting a compiled .so during plugin development
  • Package manager or updater refreshing bundled Joro plugins on the same host
  • Backup/sync tooling restoring the Joro plugin directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--build-plugin"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the written .so, submit to sandbox/AV, and check whether it was preceded by a browser hit to 127.0.0.1:9090 and a joro restart. 2) Contain: quarantine the .so, stop joro before it re-opens the plugin, and isolate the host if the file is unsigned/unknown. 3) Hunt: look for joro spawning an interactive shell or making outbound public connections after the write, and sweep other operator hosts for the same .so hash (one ABI-matched plugin works against every operator on the release).

Nuclio CronJob shell runtime reads serviceaccount token via injected curl --header (CVE-2026-52831) AIInstallation High
Hunts the runtime exploitation of CVE-2026-52831: a Nuclio-generated CronJob runs '/bin/sh -c curl --header ...' where an injected header key or $(...) body substitution has broken the shell quoting and appended attacker commands that read the pod serviceaccount token. Article-specific because it anchors on the exact curl --header shape concatenated with a read of /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token or a command substitution the sink at lazy.go:2212 executes. Rationale: Anchors on the exact sink shape from lazy.go:2212 ('/bin/sh -c curl ... --header ...') combined with the article's serviceaccount token path and the $()/backtick command-substitution primitive (Path-B, lazy.go:2188); the curl+--header+token triad is not a shape legitimate cron curls emit. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/nuclio/nuclio/CVE-2026-52831/ • https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-4598
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1552.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimately authored Nuclio cron function that intentionally reads its own serviceaccount token inside the request body for a self-referential health check
  • An operator debugging a CronJob by running curl with an inline $(date) or $(hostname) substitution in a --header value
  • Backtick or $() present in a benign custom header value used for correlation IDs
  • Security scanner/pentest replaying the PoC in a sanctioned test namespace
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","liveness") and AccountName in~ ("nuclio","nobody") and ProcessCommandLine !contains "; ")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and the parent chain; confirm the parent is a Nuclio-named CronJob pod and identify the injected segment after the closing --header quote or inside $(). Capture the namespace/pod and whether the token was actually cat'd or piped outbound. 2) Contain: suspend the offending CronJob (kubectl patch cronjob ... -p '{"spec":{"suspend":true}}'), delete the parent NuclioFunction, and rotate the pod serviceaccount token / bound secrets. 3) Hunt: enumerate all CronJobs whose args contain '/bin/sh -c' + 'curl' + shell metacharacters across namespaces, and review Nuclio version — upgrade past 1.15.27 (fixed in 0.0.0-20260601075854-3356b86a8bfa).

    or ProcessCommandLine contains "$("
    or ProcessCommandLine contains "`"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName

Nuclio pod egress from injected curl/shell carrying serviceaccount token to external host (CVE-2026-52831) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects exfiltration after CVE-2026-52831 exploitation: a curl/wget/nc/shell process spawned inside a Nuclio CronJob pod makes an outbound connection to a public IP while its command line references the pod serviceaccount token path or a $() substitution — i.e. the injected payload is shipping the stolen token off-cluster. Distinct network pivot from the endpoint process detection. Rationale: Combines the injected exfil primitive (curl/nc reading the serviceaccount token or running $()) with a public-IP destination, so it only fires when the stolen token/output actually leaves the cluster — the article confirms the token path is readable and the sink is a curl invocation reaching the network. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/nuclio/nuclio/CVE-2026-52831/ • https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2026-4598
ATT&CKT1567 T1552.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Nuclio cron function that curls an external webhook and happens to include a token-bearing header from a mounted secret (not the SA token path)
  • Container image pulling telemetry/metrics to a SaaS endpoint via curl with a $() timestamp in the URL
  • Break-glass debugging where an operator curls an external paste service with dynamic content
  • NAT/egress-gateway rewriting internal IPs so the destination appears public
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl endswith ".svc.cluster.local" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination IP/URL is untrusted and correlate the same pod's process events for a preceding serviceaccount token read; capture bytes-out and whether the token value appears in the request. 2) Contain: kill the pod, suspend the parent CronJob, block the destination IP at egress, and rotate the pod serviceaccount token plus any secrets it could reach. 3) Hunt: search Kubernetes audit for API calls authenticated with that serviceaccount from off-cluster or unusual source IPs, and review whether the token was used to list secrets or modify RBAC; upgrade Nuclio past 1.15.27.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","dash","bash","nc","ncat")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
    or (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "curl" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine contains "$(")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection == "Outbound"
| where DstIpAddr !startswith "10." and DstIpAddr !startswith "192.168." and DstIpAddr !startswith "172.16."
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","sh","bash","nc","ncat")
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine contains "/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token"
        or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ActingProcessCommandLine contains "$(")
    | project DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
) on DvcHostname
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(curl OR wget OR nc OR ncat) @process.command_line:*serviceaccount/token*
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4
| ContextImageFileName=/\/(curl|wget|sh|bash|nc|ncat)$/i
| NOT cidr("10.0.0.0/8", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("172.16.0.0/12", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| NOT cidr("192.168.0.0/16", field=RemoteAddressIP4)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, RemoteAddressIP4, RemotePort], function=count())
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("curl","wget","sh","bash","nc","ncat") AND (Processes.process="*/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token*" OR (Processes.process="*curl*" AND Processes.process="*$(*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("curl","wget","sh","bash","nc","ncat") AND (Processes.process="*/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token*" OR (Processes.process="*curl*" AND Processes.process="*$(*"))) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

Install of fake Paysafe/Skrill/Neteller npm & PyPI credential-stealer packages AIInstallation High
Hunts developer/CI machines running npm or pip against the 17 named malicious payment-SDK packages (paysafe-*, skrill*, neteller) that impersonate legitimate Paysafe/Skrill/Neteller SDKs and steal API keys, AWS keys, GitHub and npm tokens. Article-specific because it keys on the exact package names published in this campaign, not generic dependency installs. Rationale: Uses the 17 exact package names Socket enumerated (paysafe-checkout, paysafe-vault, skrill-sdk, neteller, etc.) scoped to the actual package-manager binaries — high fidelity because these package names have no legitimate publisher and installation is the campaign's install step. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1204.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher intentionally detonating the packages in a sandbox to reproduce the campaign
  • An internal private-registry package that legitimately contains the substring 'skrill' or 'paysafe' in its name
  • A blue-team engineer running an IOC-validation install against a proxy that blocks the fetch
  • A dependency-audit tool that references the package names in a lockfile scan (not an actual install)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "--registry=https://your-internal-registry" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the exact package + version installed (npm 1.0.0-1.0.3 or PyPI 1.0.0 are the malicious ranges) and identify the machine/CI runner and user. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner and immediately rotate ALL secrets present on that machine — Paysafe API keys, AWS keys, GitHub tokens, npm tokens — per Socket's guidance. Deny the package names at the registry proxy. Step 3 (hunt): Search dependency trees org-wide for any of the 17 names, grep CI logs for PAYSAFE_API_KEY appearing alongside these package names, and pivot to UC2 to check for outbound exfil to the ngrok C2.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("npm.exe","npm","node.exe","pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","python3.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("paysafe-checkout","paysafe-vault","paysafe-js","paysafe-api","paysafe-node","paysafe-cards","paysafe-fraud","paysafe-kyc","paysafe-payments","paysafe-sdk","skrill-payments","skrill-sdk","skrill","neteller")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","add"," i ")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("npm","node.exe","pip","python","yarn","pnpm")
| where CommandLine has_any ("paysafe-checkout","paysafe-vault","paysafe-js","paysafe-api","paysafe-node","paysafe-cards","paysafe-fraud","paysafe-kyc","paysafe-payments","paysafe-sdk","skrill-payments","skrill-sdk","skrill","neteller")
| where CommandLine has_any ("install","add")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

C2 exfil to Paysafe-stealer ngrok endpoint caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev AICommand & Control High
Hunts any host resolving or connecting to the campaign's exfiltration endpoint caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev, the C2 the fake payment SDKs POST stolen credentials/tokens to. Article-specific because it keys on the single confirmed IOC domain from this campaign rather than the whole ngrok TLD. Rationale: Keys on the single confirmed IOC domain (caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev) from the article — a direct match is nearly always malicious since it is the stealer's dedicated exfil endpoint, giving very low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev
ATT&CKT1567 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A malware analyst or threat-intel researcher deliberately resolving the IOC for enrichment
  • A DNS sinkhole/RPZ that logs the query before blocking it (query still appears in DNS telemetry)
  • Passive DNS collectors or scanning tools crawling the ngrok subdomain
  • The ngrok free subdomain being recycled to a benign tunnel by a different user after takedown
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the host and the initiating process — correlate the connecting process (Node/Python) with UC1 to confirm one of the 17 malicious packages ran on this machine. Step 2 (contain): Block caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat all secrets on it as compromised — rotate Paysafe API keys, AWS keys, GitHub and npm tokens immediately. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep proxy/DNS logs org-wide for the same domain over 30d, review AWS CloudTrail for any use of exfiltrated AWS keys from unfamiliar IPs, and check GitHub/npm audit logs for token misuse.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "caliber-spinner-finishing.ngrok-free.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or SHA1 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or MD5 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or SHA1 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b") or MD5 in~ ("ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["ce09810adca70ebec87bc455380ef629ceaa2a0d926149d9115604060167682c", "c6af37a6739f0d919ab7049caf3a85831cab44bdbea27e0d9de7adec80334e2b"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2025-49113 RCE: Roundcube web daemon spawns shell fetching VShell loader · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SquareShell webshell dropped as Roundcube newmail_notifier/mail_preview.php · [LLM] VShell in-memory implant masquerading as kernel worker [kworker/0:2] · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] VShell C2 egress from mail server to UNK_MassTraction sslip.io infrastructure · [LLM] SquareShell webshell interaction via HTTP request to mail_preview.php · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
SquareShell webshell dropped as Roundcube newmail_notifier/mail_preview.php AIInstallation High
Hunts creation of the SquareShell PHP webshell that UNK_MassTraction installs after exploiting CVE-2025-49113, masquerading inside the legitimate Roundcube newmail_notifier plugin directory as mail_preview.php. The genuine newmail_notifier plugin ships no such file, so a web-server user writing it is a webshell drop. Rationale: Uses the exact webshell path plugins/newmail_notifier/mail_preview.php confirmed in Proofpoint's IOC list; the real newmail_notifier plugin has no mail_preview.php, so any write of that file by the web daemon is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against Proofpoint blog and CVE-2025-49113 advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/one-email-closer-edge-unkmasstraction-physics-exploitation • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8j8w-wwqc-x596 • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/suspected-china-aligned-hackers-exploit.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Roundcube plugin/theme update or reinstall by a package manager writing PHP files into plugins
  • Administrator manually editing/deploying a custom newmail_notifier plugin file
  • Backup/restore of the webroot re-writing .php files under /var/www
  • Configuration-management tooling (Ansible/Puppet) templating PHP into the plugins directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("apt","apt-get","dpkg","yum","dnf","rpm","composer","git","rsync","tar")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the dropped file and hash it; confirm mail_preview.php does not belong to the upstream newmail_notifier plugin and inspect for system/exec/passthru/shell_exec/assert/popen. Identify the writing process (php-fpm/apache) and preceding requests. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, isolate the mail server from egress, and rotate all Roundcube/IMAP credentials and session secrets (des_key) as sessions may be stolen. 3) Hunt: review web-access logs for GET/POST to newmail_notifier/mail_preview.php, look for a child shell spawned by the web daemon, and pivot to outbound connections to 45.150.109.151 / 194.213.18.133 / 45.86.229.111 and *.sslip.io.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mail_preview.php" or (FileName endswith ".php" and FolderPath has "newmail_notifier")
| where FolderPath has_any ("roundcube","roundcubemail","newmail_notifier","/plugins/","/var/www")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "mail_preview.php" or (TargetFileName endswith ".php" and TargetFilePath has "newmail_notifier")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CVE-2025-49113 RCE: Roundcube web daemon spawns shell fetching VShell loader AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2025-49113 Crypt_GPG_Engine deserialization RCE outcome where the Roundcube PHP/web process (php-fpm, apache2, httpd, nginx) spawns a shell or download tool that pulls the SNOWLIGHT/VShell loader from the campaign C2 (sslip.io:23088/app/js/jquery.min.js or 45.86.229.111/slw). Anchors on web-daemon parent plus the campaign C2 strings so it fires on the specific chain, not generic shell use. Rationale: Pairs the web-daemon parent (the CVE-2025-49113 execution context, which runs as the web user) with the exact campaign C2 strings from Proofpoint's IOC list (sslip.io:23088/app/js/jquery.min.js, 45.86.229.111/slw). The C2-string requirement drives FP to near zero. Cross-checked against Proofpoint blog and Sysdig VShell/UNC5174 write-up. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/one-email-closer-edge-unkmasstraction-physics-exploitation • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/unc5174-chinese-threat-actor-vshell • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8j8w-wwqc-x596
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Roundcube plugin invoking curl/wget to an internal update mirror (would not contain the campaign C2 strings)
  • Monitoring/APM agent shelling out from a web worker (no sslip.io / campaign-IP match)
  • Security scanner replaying the CVE-2025-49113 PoC during an authorized pentest
  • Admin debugging PHP by running shell commands under the www-data user
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "internal-mirror" and ProcessCommandLine !has "127.0.0.1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the parent PHP request; confirm the destination is a campaign IP/sslip.io host and whether the download succeeded (check for the fetched jquery.min.js on disk / in memory). 2) Contain: kill the process tree, block egress to 45.150.109.151, 194.213.18.133, 45.86.229.111 and *.sslip.io:23088, and isolate the host — VShell loads in memory so a reboot may be needed to clear the implant. 3) Hunt: look for a masqueraded [kworker/0:2] process, the mail_preview.php webshell, new IMAP/webmail sessions from unusual IPs, and lateral movement or port-forwarding from the mail server into the internal network.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("apache2","httpd","php-fpm","php","php-cgi","nginx")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sslip.io","45.150.109.151","194.213.18.133","45.86.229.111","jquery.min.js","/slw","| sh","|sh","| bash","|bash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("apache2","httpd","php-fpm","php","php-cgi","nginx")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","python","perl")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sslip.io","45.150.109.151","194.213.18.133","45.86.229.111","jquery.min.js","/slw","| sh","|sh","| bash","|bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VShell C2 egress from mail server to UNK_MassTraction sslip.io infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on outbound connections to the confirmed UNK_MassTraction / VShell C2 endpoints: IPs 45.150.109.151, 194.213.18.133, 45.86.229.111 and the IP-encoding domains 45.150.109.151.sslip.io / 194.213.18.133.sslip.io (port 23088 and 8080). Catches both mail-server VShell beaconing and IceCube in-browser exfil to the same infrastructure. Rationale: Ships the three C2 IPs and the two IP-encoding sslip.io domains confirmed in Proofpoint's IOC block (also carried on ports 23088 and 8080). Static IOCs with essentially no legitimate reason for a university mail server to contact, so low FP. Corroborated by Proofpoint primary blog and second-source reporting on VShell/sslip.io C2 tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/one-email-closer-edge-unkmasstraction-physics-exploitation • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/unc5174-chinese-threat-actor-vshell • https://www.theregister.com/security/2026/07/08/suspected-chinese-snoops-caught-breaking-into-universities-roundcube-mailservers/5268778
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox appliance deliberately detonating the sample and beaconing to the C2 (expected from a sinkhole/analysis host)
  • Security researcher validating the IOCs from a lab box
  • Another tenant reusing the same sslip.io wildcard for benign purposes (rare — sslip.io encodes the destination IP, so the domains map to the same attacker IPs)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host and the process/user that initiated the connection (mail-server VShell vs. workstation browser running IceCube). 2) Contain: block the three IPs and *.sslip.io at the perimeter, isolate the source host, and revoke Roundcube sessions/tokens if the source is a mail server. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for any prior connection to these IPs/domains over 90 days, correlate to the mail_preview.php webshell and web-daemon-spawned shells, and check for port-forwarding/SOCKS sessions establishing internal pivots from the mail server.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.150.109.151","194.213.18.133","45.86.229.111")
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("45.150.109.151.sslip.io","194.213.18.133.sslip.io")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, LocalIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("45.150.109.151","194.213.18.133","45.86.229.111")
    or DstHostname in~ ("45.150.109.151.sslip.io","194.213.18.133.sslip.io")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

VShell in-memory implant masquerading as kernel worker [kworker/0:2] AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a user-space process presenting the process name '[kworker/0:2]' — the disguise Proofpoint reports the in-memory VShell implant uses on compromised Roundcube servers. Genuine kworker entries are kernel threads with no on-disk image, parent PID 2, and no network; a userland binary or one making egress under that name is the implant. Rationale: Uses the exact VShell process-masquerade name '[kworker/0:2]' from Proofpoint's malware analysis. Real kworkers are kernel threads (no image path, parented to kthreadd/PID 2); the queries require a real on-disk image path, isolating the impostor. Tier=hunting because the presented process name depends on the collector capturing prctl-set comm names. Cross-checked against Proofpoint blog and VShell tradecraft reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/one-email-closer-edge-unkmasstraction-physics-exploitation • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/unc5174-chinese-threat-actor-vshell
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1620
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • EDR/telemetry parsing quirk surfacing a genuine kernel thread with an inferred image path
  • A benign monitoring script literally containing the string [kworker/0:2] in an argument (e.g. grepping process lists)
  • Custom kernel-tuning tooling referencing kworker names
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !in~ ("/proc","") and isnotempty(SHA256)
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the host, compare against /proc — confirm the PID has a real /proc/<pid>/exe and network sockets (kernel workers have neither); dump the process memory for VShell/Go strings. 2) Contain: isolate the host and capture volatile memory before reboot (VShell is memory-resident); block the campaign C2 IPs. 3) Hunt: correlate the masqueraded process to the web-daemon-spawned loader, the mail_preview.php webshell, and outbound sessions to *.sslip.io; check for interactive shell and port-forwarding activity from the same PID.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "[kworker/0:2]" or FileName == "[kworker/0:2]"
| where isnotempty(FolderPath) and FolderPath !startswith "/proc"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "[kworker/0:2]" or ActingProcessName =~ "[kworker/0:2]"
| where isnotempty(ActingProcessName)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, SHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SquareShell webshell interaction via HTTP request to mail_preview.php AICommand & Control High
Alerts on any web request to plugins/newmail_notifier/mail_preview.php on a Roundcube host — the SquareShell webshell endpoint Proofpoint identified. Because the legitimate newmail_notifier plugin exposes no such endpoint, any GET/POST to it indicates operator interaction with the webshell (post-CVE-2025-49113 remote code execution). Rationale: Matches the exact webshell URI plugins/newmail_notifier/mail_preview.php from Proofpoint's IOCs; unlike the deserialization POST body, this path appears in web-access logs, making it directly detectable. Distinct log-source pivot (web/access logs) from the file-drop and process UCs. defender_kql left empty because HTTP access logs are not a Defender Advanced Hunting table; use Sentinel ImWebSession/W3CIISLog or the CIM Web datamodel. Cross-checked against: • https://www.proofpoint.com/us/blog/threat-insight/one-email-closer-edge-unkmasstraction-physics-exploitation • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-8j8w-wwqc-x596
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vulnerability scanner probing known webshell paths during an authorized assessment
  • DFIR/IR team manually browsing to the file to confirm the compromise
  • Web crawler or monitoring tool following a link to the plugins directory (would return 404 if the shell is absent — filter on 200 status to reduce noise)
Suppression filter
| where HttpStatusCode == 200
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source IP and user-agent hitting mail_preview.php and whether the response was 200 (webshell present and answering); pull the request body/query for command strings. 2) Contain: remove the webshell file, block the source IP if external, and rotate Roundcube/IMAP credentials and session secrets. 3) Hunt: reconstruct the operator's command history from access logs, pivot to any child processes spawned by the web daemon and outbound C2 to the sslip.io infrastructure, and check for VShell ([kworker/0:2]) persistence.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Url has "newmail_notifier/mail_preview.php"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-42009", "CVE-2025-49113")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2024-42009", "CVE-2025-49113")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07

description: |

    object payload signature.
references:

logsource:
    category: process_creation

detection:

            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'

            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'

falsepositives:

level: high

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

        where DNS.query IN ("45.150.109.151.sslip.io", "194.213.18.133.sslip.io")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or SHA1 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or MD5 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or SHA1 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0") or MD5 in~ ("a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a02f124c5ce4180bd130a62ee03262f399c33491de3aed36e0b15155ae4926c0"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

High

AI Coding Agents Found Triggering Endpoint Security Rules Built to Catch Attackers

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Sophos looked at a week of its own endpoint data and found that AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenAI Codex are setting off detection rules written to catch human intruders. The agents are not malicious. They just do a lot of things that, to a behavioral engine, look exactly like an attack. Decrypting browser credentials, listing what sits in Windows' credential store,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] certutil-blocked-then-bitsadmin LOLBin download pivot on same host
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Claude Code launched with --dangerously-skip-permissions guardrail bypass · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — AI Coding Agents Found Triggering Endpoint Security Rules Built to Catch Attacke
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Startup-folder script drop via PowerShell (Cursor persistence pattern) · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] DPAPI browser-credential decrypt via PowerShell (GStack /browse skill under AI coding agent) · [LLM] Windows Credential Manager enumeration via cmdkey /list under coding agent · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
DPAPI browser-credential decrypt via PowerShell (GStack /browse skill under AI coding agent) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the exact PowerShell one-liner GStack's /browse skill runs under Claude Code/Cursor to unlock Chromium credential data: Add-Type System.Security then ProtectedData::Unprotect on a base64 blob. Detects browser-credential decryption regardless of whether an AI agent or an attacker drove it, while surfacing the agent parent for triage. Rationale: Uses the verbatim GStack /browse command signature from the Sophos blog (ProtectedData::Unprotect + FromBase64String under powershell), which is the highest-fidelity string in the article; the AgentLineage tag distinguishes benign agent automation from real theft without dropping either. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer's Claude Code running GStack /browse for legitimate browser automation
  • Password managers or browser-profile migration utilities that legitimately DPAPI-decrypt saved logins
  • Authorized red-team/pentest tooling exercising browser credential extraction
  • Security research or QA reproducing the Sophos finding
  • Backup/sync tooling re-protecting DPAPI blobs on the same user context
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcessParentFileName — if the parent is claude.exe/cursor.exe/codex it is likely benign agent automation; confirm the logged-on user actually runs a coding agent. 2) Contain: if the parent is NOT a known agent (real theft), isolate the host and force-reset the browser-stored credentials and any SSO sessions decrypted. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for cmdkey /list, certutil/bitsadmin downloads, and startup-folder writes within the same session to separate agent noise from an intrusion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "Unprotect"
    and ProcessCommandLine has "FromBase64String"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe","node.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where CommandLine has "System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData" and CommandLine has "Unprotect" and CommandLine has "FromBase64String"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| extend AgentLineage = iff(ParentProcessName has_any ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, AgentLineage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: DPAPI Browser Credential Decryption via PowerShell (GStack browse skill)
id: 6f1d2a94-8c3b-4a11-9e0f-7d2c5b4a1e33
description: Detects the GStack /browse skill's PowerShell that calls DPAPI ProtectedData.Unprotect on a base64 blob to decrypt Chromium browser credentials, observed running under Claude Code/Cursor and equally used for real browser-credential theft.
references:
  - https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ai-coding-agents-found-triggering.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1059.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData'
      - 'Unprotect'
      - 'FromBase64String'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate GStack /browse browser automation by a developer's Claude Code
  - Password-manager or profile-migration tooling that decrypts DPAPI blobs
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe OR *\pwsh.exe) @CommandLine:(*ProtectedData* AND *Unprotect* AND *FromBase64String*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/System\.Security\.Cryptography\.ProtectedData/i
| CommandLine=/Unprotect/i
| CommandLine=/FromBase64String/i
| agent := if(ParentBaseFileName=/(claude|cursor|codex|node)\.exe/i, "ai-agent", "other")
| table([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ParentBaseFileName, agent, ImageFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData*" AND Processes.process="*Unprotect*" AND Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval likely_agent=if(match(parent_process_name,"(?i)(claude|cursor|codex|node)\.exe"),"AI coding agent","other") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*System.Security.Cryptography.ProtectedData*" AND Processes.process="*Unprotect*" AND Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval likely_agent=if(match(parent_process_name,"(?i)(claude|cursor|codex|node)\.exe"),"AI coding agent","other") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime) | sort - lastTime
Windows Credential Manager enumeration via cmdkey /list under coding agent AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts cmdkey.exe /list — Claude Code was observed enumerating everything Windows Credential Manager holds. Rare in normal user space; the AI-agent parent lineage is surfaced to separate benign agent recon from an attacker's credential survey. Rationale: cmdkey.exe /list is the literal command Sophos attributed to Claude Code enumerating Credential Manager; it is uncommon enough in user space to hunt broadly while tagging agent lineage for fast triage. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry • https://cyberpress.org/endpoint-rules-claude-code-cursor-codex-lolbin/
ATT&CKT1555.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin auditing saved RDP / network credentials with cmdkey /list
  • Logon or provisioning scripts that inventory stored credentials
  • MDM/endpoint-management agents enumerating credential entries
  • A developer's coding agent legitimately checking cached credentials before an automation task
  • IT troubleshooting of Credential Manager / SSO issues
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent chain — a claude.exe/cursor.exe ancestor plus a developer user strongly implies benign agent recon; an interactive shell under a service or unexpected user warrants escalation. 2) Contain: if paired with credential decryption or exfil, isolate the host and rotate any credentials visible in Credential Manager for that user. 3) Hunt: search the same host/session for DPAPI browser decrypt (UC1), LOLBin downloads, and outbound connections to determine if enumeration led to use.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "cmdkey.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/list"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend AgentLineage = iff(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, AgentLineage
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmdkey.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/list"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| extend AgentLineage = iff(ParentProcessName has_any ("claude.exe","cursor.exe","codex.exe"), "AI coding agent", "other")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, AgentLineage
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Windows Credential Manager Enumeration via cmdkey /list
id: 2a7c9e40-1b6d-4f28-8c11-3e9a5d7b4c20
description: Detects cmdkey.exe /list enumerating stored Windows Credential Manager entries, observed under Claude Code and used by attackers for credential discovery.
references:
  - https://www.sophos.com/en-us/blog/2607_agents_vs_telemetry
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/ai-coding-agents-found-triggering.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering

logsource:
