Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48282", "CVE-2026-56290", "CVE-2026-55255", "CVE-2026-48908", "CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2025-3248")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-48282", "CVE-2026-56290", "CVE-2026-55255", "CVE-2026-48908", "CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2025-3248")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-48282", "CVE-2026-56290", "CVE-2026-55255", "CVE-2026-48908", "CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2025-3248")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2026-48282", "CVE-2026-56290", "CVE-2026-55255", "CVE-2026-48908", "CVE-2026-33017", "CVE-2025-3248")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

15-Year-Old GhostLock Flaw Enables Root and Container Escape on Most Linux Distros

The Hacker News
2026-07-08 8 use cases 3 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Researchers at&nbsp;Nebula Security&nbsp;have disclosed GhostLock (CVE-2026-43499), a 15-year-old Linux kernel flaw that lets any logged-in user take full&nbsp;root&nbsp;control of a machine that has not been patched. The vulnerable code has shipped by default in essentially every mainstream distribution since 2011. The flaw needs no special permission, no unusual settings, and no network

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Host exposure to GhostLock IonStack kernel-to-root chain CVEs (CVE-2026-43499 et al.) · [LLM] Linux unprivileged process escalates to root without sudo/su/pkexec (kernel-LPE / container-escape shape)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Host exposure to GhostLock IonStack kernel-to-root chain CVEs (CVE-2026-43499 et al.) AIExploitation High
Surfaces every managed asset whose vulnerability inventory reports exposure to the GhostLock/IonStack chain and its sibling 2026 Linux LPE CVEs, so multi-tenant/cloud/CI hosts (where a local foothold is most likely) can be patched first. Article-specific because it keys on the exact CVE identifiers Nebula disclosed and the fix-regression CVE the article warns you must also clear. Rationale: Uses the five concrete CVE IDs named in the article/pre-extracted IOCs (GhostLock CVE-2026-43499, the Firefox first-half CVE-2026-10702, sibling Bad Epoll CVE-2026-46242, KEV-listed Copy Fail CVE-2026-31431, and the fix-regression CVE-2026-53166). TVM inventory match is deterministic; corroborated fixed-kernel version (Linux 7.1) confirms which builds clear it. Cross-checked against: • https://nebusec.ai/research/ionstack-part-2/ • https://securityonline.info/ghostlock-cve-2026-43499/ • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-43499 • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/05/01/cve-2026-31431-copy-fail-vulnerability-enables-linux-root-privilege-escalation/
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Host already patched to fixed kernel but TVM inventory snapshot is stale (rescan pending)
  • Kernel live-patching (kpatch/ksplice/kernelcare) applied at runtime while the on-disk package version still reads vulnerable
  • Ephemeral CI/build containers flagged that are torn down within minutes and never expose a persistent foothold
  • CVE-2026-10702 reported against Firefox on single-user endpoints that are lower priority than shared/multi-tenant Linux hosts
  • Air-gapped or single-tenant hosts where the 'already logged in' precondition is low-risk
Response runbook
1) Triage: rank hits by exposure — shared/multi-tenant Linux hosts, cloud servers, container hosts and CI runners first (the footholds the article calls out); confirm the running kernel via OSVersion, not just package metadata (live-patch can mask it). 2) Contain: schedule/deploy the current distribution kernel (Linux 7.1+ / vendor-fixed build that also clears the CVE-2026-53166 regression) and reboot; where patching lags, enable RANDOMIZE_KSTACK_OFFSET and STATIC_USERMODE_HELPER as interim hardening. 3) Hunt: on any host that stayed vulnerable and internet-adjacent, run the companion non-root-to-root behavioral hunt and review for post-exploitation persistence (new root cron, added users, SSH authorized_keys).

Linux unprivileged process escalates to root without sudo/su/pkexec (kernel-LPE / container-escape shape) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the article's core outcome: a non-root user's process yielding a child running as root without transiting a legitimate setuid escalation helper, the observable signature of a kernel use-after-free exploit like GhostLock that 'enables root and container escape.' Not tied to a phishing/LOLBin template; anchors on the unprivileged-to-root process transition on Linux endpoints. Rationale: Grounded in the article's central, repeatedly-stated claim ('enables root and container escape on most Linux distros' from 'any local program'). The non-root-parent-to-root-child transition without a setuid helper is the observable residue of a kernel UAF LPE; escalation/setuid binaries are excluded to raise fidelity. Datadog left empty because the listed linux.auditd normalized fields do not cleanly expose the euid/auid transition this detection needs. Cross-checked against: • https://nebusec.ai/research/ionstack-part-2/ • https://securityonline.info/ghostlock-cve-2026-43499/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/cisa-adds-actively-exploited-linux-root.html
ATT&CKT1068 T1611
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User-invoked setuid-root binaries not in the exclusion list (e.g. Xorg, exim, at, dbus helpers, vendor VPN/backup agents) reporting effective root
  • Container runtimes (runc, crun, containerd-shim, docker-init) launching root workloads whose immediate parent is a non-root orchestrator process
  • User crontab entries or systemd user units configured to execute a root helper
  • Interactive 'sudo -i' / policy-kit GUI prompts whose telemetry attributes the child to the invoking user rather than the helper
  • Configuration-management agents (Ansible/Salt/Puppet) escalating via a custom become-method not covered by su/sudo/pkexec
Suppression filter
| where not (ParentProcess in~ ("ansible","salt-minion","puppet","chef-client","dockerd","docker-init","crun") or ChildProcess in~ ("Xorg","exim","at","dbus-daemon-launch-helper","vpnagentd"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full parent->child tree and both command lines; confirm the child genuinely ran as uid 0 and the parent was an ordinary user process (not a setuid helper), and cross-check whether the host is still exposed to the GhostLock chain via the companion TVM hunt. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture a memory/disk snapshot before reboot, and terminate the root-context shell/process; rotate any credentials or keys reachable from that host. 3) Hunt: sweep the fleet for the same non-root->root pattern, and on confirmed hosts look for follow-on persistence (new root cron, added /etc/passwd or sudoers entries, injected SSH authorized_keys) and container-escape indicators (containerized PID writing to host mount paths).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName =~ "root"
| where isnotempty(InitiatingProcessAccountName) and InitiatingProcessAccountName !~ "root"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","gksudo","gksu","runuser","login","sshd","systemd","init","runc","containerd-shim","crond","cron","polkitd","lightdm","gdm","sddm")
| where FileName !in~ ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","passwd","chsh","chfn","gpasswd","newgrp","mount","umount","fusermount","fusermount3","ping","ping6","ntfs-3g","pmount","mount.nfs")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RanAsUser = AccountName, ParentUser = InitiatingProcessAccountName, ParentProcess = InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildProcess = FileName, ChildCmd = ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetUsername =~ "root"
| where isnotempty(ActorUsername) and ActorUsername !~ "root"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","runuser","login","sshd","systemd","runc","containerd-shim","polkitd","crond"))
| where not(TargetProcessName has_any ("sudo","su","pkexec","sudoedit","doas","passwd","chsh","chfn","gpasswd","newgrp","mount","umount","fusermount","ping","ntfs-3g"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 UserName=root
| ParentBaseFileName!=/^(sudo|su|pkexec|sudoedit|doas|runuser|login|sshd|systemd|init|runc|containerd-shim.*|cron|crond|polkitd)$/i
| ImageFileName=/\/(bash|dash|sh|zsh|ksh|python[0-9.]*|perl|ruby|ncat|nc|busybox)$/i

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent

Accenture confirms breach after hacker offers stolen data for sale

BleepingComputer
2026-07-07 6 use cases 2 techniques 3 kill-chain phases detected

IT services giant Accenture has confirmed it suffered a security breach after a threat actor claimed to have stolen 35 GB of source code and other data from the company. [...]

ATT&CKT1190 T1486
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix
Phase 1
Reconnaissance

Detected

Exploitation
Detected

Installation

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] First-seen network origin authenticating to Azure DevOps resource
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Anomalous Azure Storage account key listing (listKeys) by first-seen caller · [LLM] Bulk Azure DevOps repository clone/download by a single identity · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Anomalous Azure Storage account key listing (listKeys) by first-seen caller AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts an identity enumerating Azure Storage account access keys via the ARM listKeys action from a principal/IP not seen doing so in the baseline window. Mirrors the '888' Accenture theft where Azure Storage access keys were harvested for offline data-plane access to blobs/config. Rationale: Article states 'Azure Storage access keys' were stolen; the ARM operation that exposes them is the concrete string Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action, and a first-seen-caller anti-join surfaces harvest activity without an IOC. Cross-checked against Microsoft's own Azure-Sentinel Anomalous_Listing_Of_Storage_Keys hunting query. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/accenture-confirms-breach-after-hacker-offers-stolen-data-for-sale/ • https://github.com/Azure/Azure-Sentinel/blob/master/Solutions/Azure%20Activity/Hunting%20Queries/Anomalous_Listing_Of_Storage_Keys.yaml • https://orca.security/resources/blog/azure-shared-key-authorization-exploitation/
ATT&CKT1528 T1580
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Terraform/Bicep IaC deployments or CI service principals that legitimately call listKeys during storage provisioning
  • Backup/monitoring tooling (e.g. Veeam, storage-explorer, azcopy setup) rotating or reading keys
  • A newly onboarded platform-engineering account performing first-time storage administration
  • Azure Policy or Defender for Cloud remediation runbooks that enumerate keys
  • Break-glass admin performing genuine incident cleanup after this very breach
Suppression filter
| where Caller !endswith "@yourtenant.onmicrosoft.com" or Caller has "#EXT#"   // keep external/guest and non-standard callers; append a known-automation SPN allow-list here
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve Caller to a human vs service principal; check whether the SourceIPs and ASN match known corporate/CI egress, and whether the same Caller has recent risky Entra sign-ins. 2) Contain: if the caller is unexpected, rotate the affected storage account keys immediately (both key1/key2) and disable/rotate the caller's credentials or the SPN secret; enable Shared Key access restrictions where possible. 3) Hunt: pivot on the storage accounts named in _ResourceId for subsequent data-plane blob reads (StorageBlobLogs) from IPs differing from the management-plane caller, and correlate the same Caller against Azure DevOps access and PAT creation in the same window.
let lookback = 14d;
let recent = 1d;
let Baseline = AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
| where OperationNameValue =~ "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action"
| where ActivityStatusValue in ("Success","Succeeded")
| summarize by Caller;
AzureActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(recent)
| where OperationNameValue =~ "Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action"
| where ActivityStatusValue in ("Success","Succeeded")
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on Caller
| summarize KeyListOps = count(), StorageAccounts = dcount(_ResourceId), SourceIPs = make_set(CallerIpAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by Caller
| where KeyListOps >= 3     // 3 = strips single benign key reads; tune to your automation baseline
| order by KeyListOps desc
source:azure.activity_logs @operationName.value:Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action @properties.activityStatusValue:Success
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as key_list_ops, values(All_Changes.object) as storage_accounts, values(All_Changes.src) as src_ips, min(_time) as firstSeen from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action" All_Changes.status IN ("success","Succeeded") by All_Changes.user _time span=1d | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | where key_list_ops >= 3 | sort - key_list_ops
| tstats summariesonly=false count as key_list_ops, values(All_Changes.object) as storage_accounts, values(All_Changes.src) as src_ips, min(_time) as firstSeen from datamodel=Change.All_Changes where All_Changes.command="Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts/listKeys/action" All_Changes.status IN ("success","Succeeded") by All_Changes.user _time span=1d | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Changes)` | where key_list_ops >= 3 | sort - key_list_ops
Bulk Azure DevOps repository clone/download by a single identity AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts a single identity performing a high volume of Azure DevOps repository clone/download/Git-read operations via Defender for Cloud Apps activity, matching the '888' actor's full clone of the internal 'AtriasTalentAcademy' repo to stage ~35GB of source for exfiltration. Rationale: Article's supporting screenshot shows the actor cloning the Azure DevOps repo '121123_AtriasTalentAcademy'; Defender for Cloud Apps is the telemetry that captures connected-app (Azure DevOps) repository read/clone activity, and a per-identity volume threshold isolates bulk staging from normal dev pulls. Microsoft confirms clone is now logged as an access event. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/accenture-confirms-breach-after-hacker-offers-stolen-data-for-sale/ • https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/release-notes/roadmap/track-repo-cloning • https://www.technadu.com/accenture-data-allegedly-listed-for-sale-on-hacking-forum-35gb-source-code-claimed-stolen/630523/
ATT&CKT1213.003 T1213
Data sources
Expected false positives — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • CI/CD build agents or self-hosted pipeline runners cloning many repos every build cycle
  • A developer performing a fresh workstation setup and cloning the full team's repo set
  • Migration/backup tooling exporting repositories in bulk
  • New team lead onboarding who clones every project they were granted
  • Automated code-scanning/SAST platforms (e.g. SonarQube, Snyk) pulling all repos
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !has "Build Service" and AccountDisplayName !has "Project Collection"   // drop Azure DevOps built-in pipeline identities
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether AccountObjectId belongs to a service/build identity (expected high volume) or an interactive user; review SourceIPs against corporate/CI egress and check the repos in ObjectName for sensitivity. 2) Contain: if unexpected, revoke the identity's Azure DevOps PATs and sessions, suspend the account, and restrict the org to conditional-access/allow-listed IPs. 3) Hunt: enumerate all repos the identity touched, check for accompanying PAT creation and storage-key listing by the same principal, and scan the cloned repos' history for embedded RSA/SSH keys and Azure secrets that now require rotation.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where Application has "DevOps"
| where ActionType has_any ("Clone","Download","Git","Repository","Export")
| summarize Actions = count(), DistinctRepos = dcount(ObjectName), ActionTypes = make_set(ActionType, 20), SourceIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp) by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where DistinctRepos >= 5 or Actions >= 50     // 5 repos / 50 ops = bulk staging, well above interactive dev browsing
| order by Actions desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
CloudAppEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Application has "DevOps"
| where ActionType has_any ("Clone","Download","Git","Repository","Export")
| summarize Actions = count(), DistinctRepos = dcount(ObjectName), ActionTypes = make_set(ActionType, 20), SourceIPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId
| where DistinctRepos >= 5 or Actions >= 50     // 5 repos / 50 ops = bulk staging, well above interactive dev browsing
| order by Actions desc
First-seen network origin authenticating to Azure DevOps resource AIDelivery Medium
Hunts a successful sign-in to the Azure DevOps resource from an ASN/country never previously seen for that user in the baseline window — the token/valid-account access that preceded the '888' repository clone. Complements PAT theft where the compromised identity pivots into the DevOps tenant from attacker infrastructure. Rationale: Article confirms 'Azure PAT (personal access tokens)' were stolen and used to reach an Azure DevOps repo under an accenture.com host; a per-user first-seen-ASN/country anti-join on sign-ins to the ResourceDisplayName 'Azure DevOps' catches the token-holder pivoting in from new infrastructure without needing an IOC. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/accenture-confirms-breach-after-hacker-offers-stolen-data-for-sale/ • https://www.technadu.com/accenture-data-allegedly-listed-for-sale-on-hacking-forum-35gb-source-code-claimed-stolen/630523/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote/travelling developers signing in from a new country or hotel/mobile ASN
  • Corporate VPN or SASE egress rotating to a new provider ASN not in the baseline
  • Contractors or new hires whose first DevOps sign-in has no baseline
  • Home-ISP changes or CGNAT reassignments shifting a user's ASN
  • Approved third-party integrations/OAuth apps authenticating to Azure DevOps from a cloud provider ASN
Suppression filter
| where IsAnonymousProxy == true or RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("high","medium")   // Defender: prioritise anonymised/risky origins over routine travel
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify with the user (or their manager) whether the new country/ASN is expected travel; check the same session for MFA satisfaction, RiskLevelDuringSignIn, and IsAnonymousProxy. 2) Contain: if unverified, revoke the user's refresh tokens and Azure DevOps PATs, force password reset + re-MFA, and apply a conditional-access location restriction to the Azure DevOps app. 3) Hunt: correlate this identity with bulk repo clone (UC above) and storage-key listing in the same window; enumerate PATs the account created and repos it accessed to scope exposure.
let lookback = 14d;
let recent = 1d;
let Baseline = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
| where ResourceDisplayName has "DevOps"
| summarize by AccountUpn, Country;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(recent)
| where ResourceDisplayName has "DevOps"
| where ErrorCode == 0
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on AccountUpn, Country
| project Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, IsAnonymousProxy
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 14d;
let recent = 1d;
let Baseline = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
| where ResourceDisplayName has "DevOps"
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize by UserPrincipalName, AutonomousSystemNumber;
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(recent)
| where ResourceDisplayName has "DevOps"
| where ResultType == 0
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on UserPrincipalName, AutonomousSystemNumber
| extend Country = tostring(parse_json(tostring(LocationDetails)).countryOrRegion)
| project TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, IPAddress, AutonomousSystemNumber, Country, AppDisplayName, ResourceDisplayName, ClientAppUsed, RiskLevelDuringSignIn
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.appDisplayName:(*DevOps* OR *devops*)
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as auths, values(Authentication.src) as src_ips, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app="Azure DevOps" by Authentication.user, Authentication.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | sort - firstSeen
| tstats summariesonly=false count as auths, values(Authentication.src) as src_ips, min(_time) as firstSeen, max(_time) as lastSeen from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication where Authentication.action=success Authentication.app="Azure DevOps" by Authentication.user, Authentication.src | `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)` | sort - firstSeen
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

      a known-admin-host watchlist

Sha1-Hulud 2.0 npm worm payload files (setup_bun.js / bun_environment.js) written or executed AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the hardcoded self-propagating payload files the Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon npm worm drops during a malicious package preinstall, matched by exact filename and known SHA256. The article cites Sha1-Hulud dumping harvested credentials into public GitHub repos as the exfiltration destination it warns about; this catches the worm at the execution stage before that exfil happens. Rationale: Uses the exact worm payload filenames (setup_bun.js, bun_environment.js) and four published SHA256 hashes from Datadog/Microsoft analyses of Sha1-Hulud 2.0 — the campaign the article names as the archetype of GitHub-hosted secret exfiltration. Filename+hash makes this alerting-grade. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating a captured Sha1-Hulud sample in a sandbox VONM
  • Threat-intel/malware-repo mirror syncing sample files to a scanning host
  • EDR test/purple-team exercise seeding the named hashes
  • A benign project legitimately shipping a file literally named setup_bun.js (rare; hash filter avoids this)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\MalwareSamples\\","\\Quarantine\\"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the SHA256 matches a known worm hash and identify the InitiatingProcess (should be node/npm/bun preinstall). Pull the parent package name and package.json to find the poisoned dependency. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner, revoke any npm/GitHub/cloud tokens present on it, and freeze the developer's npm publish rights. Step 3 (hunt): Search the org for the same hashes and for any public GitHub repos with description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.'; rotate every secret reachable from the affected build.

Cloud IMDS credential harvesting by node/npm/bun during package install (Sha1-Hulud/Megalodon) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a JavaScript package-manager process (node, npm, bun, yarn, pnpm) reaching the cloud instance-metadata service (169.254.169.254 or metadata.google.internal) — the multi-cloud credential-harvest step of the Sha1-Hulud worm. This is the 'secret theft that never touches github.com' the article says public monitoring cannot see. Rationale: Combines the concrete IMDS endpoints (169.254.169.254, metadata.google.internal) documented by Datadog/Unit42 with the JS package-manager parent context that distinguishes worm harvesting from a legitimate cloud SDK call. Pins the abuse to the install-time process rather than any app. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node.js application running on an EC2/GCE instance that legitimately queries IMDS via the AWS/GCP SDK
  • Serverless/build tooling (e.g. serverless-framework, terraform-node wrappers) resolving instance credentials
  • Cloud-native CI agents written in Node fetching a metadata-scoped token for artifact upload
  • IMDSv2 token-refresh loops from a long-running node service
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall","ci","npx") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "node_modules"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Determine whether the node/bun process was part of an npm/yarn install lifecycle (check parent chain and recent package.json changes) versus a steady-state application. Install-time IMDS access is the true positive. Step 2 (contain): Revoke the instance role's temporary credentials, quarantine the runner/host, and enforce IMDSv2 hop-limit=1 to block the container reach. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the host for setup_bun.js/bun_environment.js, trufflehog execution, and any subsequent api.github.com repo creation; rotate cloud keys the role could reach.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ASCDeviceEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "169.254.169.254" or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm","npm.cmd","bun","bun.exe","yarn","pnpm")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

TruffleHog secret scanner spawned from an npm/bun package-install context (Sha1-Hulud) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for the TruffleHog secret-discovery binary launched as a child of a JavaScript package manager or a shell inside an install script — the on-disk credential-sweep stage of the Sha1-Hulud worm. Distinct from sanctioned CI secret-scanning because the parent is node/npm/bun rather than a dedicated scanner job. Rationale: TruffleHog execution parented by node/bun/npm is the documented Sha1-Hulud secret-discovery step (Datadog/Wiz). The parent-process predicate separates worm-driven scans from an intentional trufflehog CI stage, keeping fidelity up. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A CI pipeline that legitimately runs trufflehog as a pre-commit/secret-scan step invoked from an npm script
  • Developer running `npx trufflehog` manually to audit a repo
  • Security tooling wrappers that shell out to trufflehog from a Node orchestrator
  • pre-commit framework invoking trufflehog via a node hook
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pre-commit","secret-scan","security-scan","gitleaks-trufflehog-step"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm trufflehog was not a sanctioned pipeline step — inspect the initiating package.json script and whether the run coincides with an npm install rather than a scan job. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host/runner and revoke tokens; if part of a build, halt the pipeline and quarantine produced artifacts. Step 3 (hunt): Correlate with IMDS access, bun payload files, and outbound api.github.com repo creation on the same host; rotate any secrets trufflehog could have read.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "trufflehog" or ProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","npm","npm.cmd","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has "trufflehog" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "trufflehog"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("node","bun","npm","yarn","pnpm","sh","bash")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious 'SHA1HULUD' self-hosted GitHub Actions runner installation / persistence AIInstallation High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm registering an attacker-controlled self-hosted GitHub Actions runner — identified by the runner name SHA1HULUD, the $HOME/.dev-env install directory, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, and the actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0 download. This is the worm turning GitHub into a persistence/C2 channel, exactly the github.com-as-infrastructure abuse the article describes. Rationale: Pins on four hard, campaign-unique strings from Datadog's Sha1-Hulud 2.0 analysis (runner name SHA1HULUD, RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1, ~/.dev-env, actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0). These do not appear in legitimate runner setups, giving alerting-grade fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/12/09/shai-hulud-2-0-guidance-for-detecting-investigating-and-defending-against-the-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1543 T1102
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An org that coincidentally uses a self-hosted runner directory named .dev-env (unlikely, and runner-name string still filters it)
  • Admin legitimately setting RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT=1 in a container runner build (would lack the SHA1HULUD name)
  • Runner version 2.330.0 downloaded during a legitimate GitHub-hosted runner upgrade (string paired with the other markers reduces this)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the runner registration name is SHA1HULUD or the install path is $HOME/.dev-env; check which GitHub org/repo the runner registered against. Step 2 (contain): Remove the runner from GitHub org settings, kill the runner process, revoke the PAT/GITHUB_TOKEN it used, and isolate the host. Step 3 (hunt): Search GitHub audit logs for self-hosted runner additions and for workflows triggered `on: discussion` with a `runs-on: self-hosted` job echoing github.event.discussion.body; enumerate other hosts with .dev-env.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SHA1HULUD","RUNNER_ALLOW_RUNASROOT",".dev-env","actions-runner-linux-x64-2.330.0")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Sha1-Hulud destructive wiper fallback (cipher /W, recursive del, shred over home dir) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts for the Sha1-Hulud worm's destructive fallback that fires when it cannot authenticate/propagate: on Windows `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%` plus `cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, and on Linux `find $HOME ... | xargs shred -uvz`. High-impact, low-frequency behaviour that turns a supply-chain compromise into data destruction. Rationale: Encodes the exact destructive commands Datadog documented for Sha1-Hulud's failure path (`cipher /W:%USERPROFILE%`, `del /F /Q /S %USERPROFILE%*`, `find $HOME ... shred -uvz`). cipher /W over a user profile and shred over $HOME are near-zero in normal ops, making impact-stage alerting reliable. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/
ATT&CKT1485 T1070.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin/GPO running `cipher /W:` to wipe free space during decommissioning (usually not scoped to %USERPROFILE% and not spawned by node)
  • Backup or forensics tooling using shred for secure deletion of scratch data
  • A cleanup script using recursive del on a temp path (USERPROFILE token filter reduces this)
  • Disk-sanitisation compliance jobs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","bun","bun.exe","sh","bash","cmd.exe","powershell.exe") or FileName =~ "cipher.exe"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the parent process — a wipe parented by node/bun/sh during an npm install is the true positive; capture the exact target path. Step 2 (contain): Immediately isolate the host from the network to stop further destruction and preserve volume shadow copies/backups; snapshot the disk. Step 3 (hunt): Confirm the Sha1-Hulud chain (bun payloads, trufflehog, IMDS, SHA1HULUD runner) on the host and across the fleet; initiate restore-from-backup and org-wide secret rotation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "cipher.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (ActingProcessName has "cipher.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "/W:")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "shred" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "-uvz")
    or (ActingProcessCommandLine has_all ("del","/F","/Q","/S") and ActingProcessCommandLine has "USERPROFILE")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CI/dev host exfiltrating to api.github.com shortly after cloud IMDS harvest (Sha1-Hulud exfil chain) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Correlates a package-manager process reaching cloud IMDS with the same host contacting api.github.com/github.com within 30 minutes — the Sha1-Hulud pattern of harvesting cloud secrets then pushing them into a newly created public GitHub repo. This directly targets the 'close the exfiltration gap' thesis of the article: catching secrets leaving CI toward github.com, not after they surface. Rationale: Chains the two documented Sha1-Hulud network behaviours (IMDS credential harvest → push to a new github.com repo) on the same host within a tight window, which is far more specific than either signal alone and maps precisely to the article's exfiltration-to-github concern. Time-window correlation makes it a hunt, not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://securitylabs.datadoghq.com/articles/shai-hulud-2.0-npm-worm/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/shai-hulud-2-0-ongoing-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/npm-supply-chain-attack/
ATT&CKT1567.001 T1552.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A Node app on a cloud VM that reads IMDS and also pushes to GitHub (e.g. a release bot / GitOps agent) within the window
  • CI runner that legitimately fetches instance credentials then interacts with the GitHub API for status checks
  • Renovate/Dependabot-style automation touching both IMDS and github.com
  • Container build that queries metadata for a token and pushes an image manifest referencing github.com
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install","preinstall","postinstall") or RemoteUrl has "api.github.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the github.com interaction — was a NEW repo created (check GitHub audit log for repo.create with an 18-char hex name or description 'Sha1-Hulud: The Second Coming.')? Confirm the IMDS call was install-time. Step 2 (contain): Delete the attacker repo, revoke the developer's GitHub token and the instance role credentials, and isolate the host/runner. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for bun payload files, trufflehog, and the SHA1HULUD runner on the host; enumerate all public repos org-wide matching the campaign description and rotate every exposed secret.

Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-07 14 use cases 10 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A cybercrime campaign combined a loader-as-a-service framework and DLL sideloading via a Go-compiled fake MpClient.dll, a novel evasion layer combination. The post Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation appeared first on Unit 42 .

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Null-byte inflated PE loader (>200 MB) written to user staging folder · [LLM] Browser-dropped .bin password-protected archive (fake software crack lure) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Vidar Stealer Unmasked: Code Signing Abuse, Go Loaders and File Inflation
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Fake Windows Defender MpClient.dll side-load (Vidar/Factory-v3 loader) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] XMRig Monero mining to pool.supportxmr.com / 136.243.203.109 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Fake Windows Defender MpClient.dll side-load (Vidar/Factory-v3 loader) AIInstallation High
Hunts the Cluster-B loader variant that ships a Go-compiled fake MpClient.dll exporting Defender API names (MpAllocMemory, MpConfigOpen, etc.) to hijack DLL search order when a legitimate Defender binary loads MpClient.dll. Fires when MpClient.dll is loaded from any path outside the genuine Windows Defender directories. Rationale: Uses the article's specific Cluster-B artefact: a Go-compiled fake MpClient.dll exporting Defender API names for search-order hijack; genuine MpClient.dll only ever loads from a 'Windows Defender' path, so any other path is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vidar-stealer-xmrig-miner-campaign-analysis/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/new-campaign-vidar-stealer-monero/ • https://malwaretips.com/threads/unit-42-researchers-exposed-a-new-vidar-campaign-using-a-loader-as-a-service-framework-dll-sideloading-with-a-go-compiled-fake-mpclient-dll.142161/
ATT&CKT1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Third-party AV/EDR ships its own module named MpClient.dll in a non-Defender path (rare)
  • Security researcher or malware-analysis VM with sample DLLs on disk being loaded manually
  • Backup/restore tooling relocating Defender platform files to a staging folder
  • Software packaging/repackaging tools extracting Defender binaries to a temp working directory
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","MsSense.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the loading process (InitiatingProcessFolderPath) and the DLL's SHA256; check whether the loader executable sits in Downloads/Temp/AppData and whether it is signed CN=justwatch[.]com or CN=bleacherreport[.]com. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loading process tree, and quarantine both the fake MpClient.dll and its parent EXE. 3) Hunt: sweep for outbound connections to pool.supportxmr.com / 136.243.203.109 (XMRig) and for Vidar credential/cookie theft on the same host and other hosts that executed the same parent hash.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe","MpCmdRun.exe","MsSense.exe")

XMRig Monero mining to pool.supportxmr.com / 136.243.203.109 AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the XMRig payload dropped by the Vidar/Factory-v3 loader beaconing to the Monero mining pool pool.supportxmr.com or the campaign IP 136.243.203.109. Network contact to this pool from an endpoint is a direct resource-hijacking indicator. Rationale: pool.supportxmr.com and 136.243.203.109 are the article's concrete XMRig C2/pool indicators; endpoint contact to a public Monero pool is high-fidelity resource-hijacking signal corroborated by an existing SigmaHQ mining-pool rule. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vidar-stealer-xmrig-miner-campaign-analysis/ • https://detection.fyi/sigmahq/sigma/network/dns/net_dns_pua_cryptocoin_mining_xmr/ • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/youtube-pirated-software-videos-deliver-triple-threat-vidar-stealer-laplas-clipper-xmrig-miner
ATT&CKT1496
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate hobbyist Monero mining by an employee on a corporate device (policy violation, not intrusion)
  • IT/security team detonating a sample in a monitored sandbox that egresses to the pool
  • Threat-intel enrichment appliance actively resolving the domain for classification
  • Shared research VM used for cryptomining benchmarking
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName/FolderPath making the connection — confirm it is not a sanctioned miner and check whether the process was dropped from a JustWatch/BleacherReport-signed loader in Downloads/Temp. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the miner process, and block pool.supportxmr.com and 136.243.203.109 at proxy/firewall. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for the fake MpClient.dll side-load and Vidar browser-credential/cookie/wallet theft; pivot org-wide on the parent loader hash and the mining IP.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "supportxmr.com" or RemoteIP == "136.243.203.109"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr == "136.243.203.109" or DstHostname has "supportxmr.com"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Null-byte inflated PE loader (>200 MB) written to user staging folder AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the Cluster-A/C Go loaders that append hundreds of MB of null bytes after the last PE section (observed up to 491 MB with only ~2.3 MB real content) to exceed sandbox/AV file-size limits. Flags oversized EXE/DLL files written into Downloads, Temp, or AppData. Rationale: Directly encodes the article's file-inflation evasion (up to 491 MB of null padding on a ~2.3 MB payload) using a size threshold on freshly dropped PE files in user staging paths; legit binaries rarely exceed 200 MB. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vidar-stealer-xmrig-miner-campaign-analysis/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/new-campaign-vidar-stealer-monero/
ATT&CKT1027.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Large legitimate installers (games, IDEs, CAD, driver bundles) downloaded to Downloads
  • Self-extracting archives or Electron app bundles that are genuinely >200 MB
  • Developer build output (large statically-linked binaries) written to AppData/Temp
  • Portable VM or emulator executables staged in a user folder
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") or FolderPath has "Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: submit the SHA256 and, if retained, inspect the file entropy/tail — genuine content followed by a long run of 0x00 padding confirms inflation; check the file's signer for CN=justwatch[.]com or CN=bleacherreport[.]com. 2) Contain: quarantine the file and isolate the host if executed. 3) Hunt: after stripping null padding (compresses to ~2.4 MB), look for the dropped fake MpClient.dll side-load, AMSI patching, and XMRig traffic to pool.supportxmr.com on this and related hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".dll"
| where FileSize > 209715200  // 200 MB; article observed null-byte padding up to 491 MB
| where FolderPath has_any ("Downloads","Temp","AppData")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, SHA256
| order by FileSize desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("exe","dll")
| where TargetFileSize > 209715200  // 200 MB; article observed padding up to 491 MB
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("Downloads","Temp","AppData")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TargetFileSize desc
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.(exe|dll)$/i
| WrittenBytes>209715200
| regex("(Downloads|Temp|AppData)", field=TargetFileName)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, WrittenBytes], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Filesystem.file_size) as file_size min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.dll") Filesystem.file_size>209715200 (Filesystem.file_path="*Downloads*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Temp*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*AppData*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Filesystem.file_size) as file_size min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_name="*.exe" OR Filesystem.file_name="*.dll") Filesystem.file_size>209715200 (Filesystem.file_path="*Downloads*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*Temp*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*AppData*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name Filesystem.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Browser-dropped .bin password-protected archive (fake software crack lure) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the campaign's delivery artefact: password-protected archives deliberately given a .bin extension to bypass email-gateway scanning and sandbox detonation, downloaded from malvertised fake-crack pages. Fires when a browser writes a .bin file to disk. Rationale: Encodes the article's specific delivery choice — password-protected archives with a .bin extension from malvertised fake-crack pages — scoped to browser-written files so it targets the download step rather than generic .bin files. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/vidar-stealer-xmrig-miner-campaign-analysis/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/new-campaign-vidar-stealer-monero/ • https://www.fortinet.com/blog/threat-research/youtube-pirated-software-videos-deliver-triple-threat-vidar-stealer-laplas-clipper-xmrig-miner
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User downloads a legitimate .bin disk image, firmware, or ROM file via browser
  • BIN/CUE game or CD image downloads from a legitimate archive site
  • Vendor firmware update packages distributed as .bin
  • Developer downloading a raw binary blob or model weights file
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has "Program Files" or InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect FileOriginUrl for a fake-crack/warez or malvertising landing domain and check whether an archiver (7zip/WinRAR) or the user subsequently extracted and launched an EXE from the .bin. 2) Contain: quarantine the .bin, block the origin domain, and warn/isolate the user host if execution followed. 3) Hunt: correlate to a JustWatch/BleacherReport-signed loader dropping a fake MpClient.dll, and to XMRig traffic to pool.supportxmr.com / 136.243.203.109 across the environment.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName endswith ".bin"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| where isnotempty(FileOriginUrl)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, FileOriginUrl, FileSize
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileExtension =~ "bin"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
