Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Better Auth OAuth refresh_token grant replayed without client_secret (CVE-2026-53512) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts POST requests to the Better Auth legacy token endpoints (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token) that carry a refresh_token grant but present no client authentication (no Basic/Bearer Authorization header) and still receive a 200. Because these plugins never verify a confidential client's client_secret on the refresh path, a leaked refresh_token + public client_id lets an attacker mint tokens indefinitely via repeated rotation. Rationale: Uses the exact vulnerable endpoints (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token), the refresh path's missing Authorization header, and the rotation-replay behaviour (repeated 200s) described in CVE-2026-53512. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail left empty — this is self-hosted Node HTTP telemetry those platforms don't ship. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/better-auth/CVE-2026-53512/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5rr4-8452-hf4v
ATT&CKT1528 T1212
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate PUBLIC clients (SPA/native + PKCE) correctly send no Authorization header on refresh — indistinguishable at the log layer without the oauthApplication client-type list
  • Aggressive mobile apps refreshing short-lived tokens every few minutes hit the >=3/hr threshold
  • Server-to-server integrations that place client_id/secret in the POST body rather than the Authorization header
  • Load-balancer or synthetic-monitoring probes that replay a stored refresh_token
Suppression filter
| where isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent) and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "HealthCheck" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "Datadog"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SrcIpAddr's full session and resolve the client_id being used; check the oauthApplication table — if that client's type is web/native/user-agent-based (confidential) it should NEVER refresh without client_secret, confirming abuse. 2) Contain: revoke the affected refresh chain — run db.deleteMany({model:"oauthAccessToken", where:[{field:"clientId", value: THAT_CLIENT_ID}]}) to invalidate all refresh tokens for the client, then rotate the client_secret. 3) Hunt: search for how the refresh_token leaked — XSS/log-capture/DB read; review the same SrcIp for prior /sso/register SSRF or access-token use at the victim user's scope.
let TokenEndpoints = dynamic(["/api/auth/oauth2/token","/api/auth/mcp/token"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has_any (TokenEndpoints)
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // no Basic/Bearer client auth on the refresh path
| where HttpStatusCode == 200                      // 200 == tokens minted successfully
| summarize Requests = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Endpoints = make_set(Url) by SrcIpAddr, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| where Requests >= 3    // 3+ = rotation replay: attacker re-redeems the rotated refresh_token repeatedly
| order by Requests desc
CLOUD
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as Requests, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime, values(Web.url) as url, values(Web.status) as status from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method="POST" (Web.uri_path="/api/auth/oauth2/token" OR Web.uri_path="/api/auth/mcp/token") Web.status=200 by Web.src, Web.http_user_agent, Web.dest _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where Requests>=3
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

SSRF via Better Auth SSO provider registration to internal endpoints (CVE-2026-53513) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the server-side fetch primitive behind CVE-2026-53513: with skipDiscovery:true, POST /sso/register and /sso/update-provider persist attacker-supplied oidcConfig.userInfoEndpoint/tokenEndpoint/jwksEndpoint URLs, which better-auth then fetches server-side during the OIDC callback. Surfaces the auth tier making outbound OIDC-shaped HTTP requests to RFC1918/loopback/link-local addresses. Rationale: Grounded in the corroborated CVE-2026-53513 mechanism: skipDiscovery:true + attacker-controlled oidcConfig endpoints on /sso/register and /sso/update-provider drive server-side fetches; the high-fidelity pivot is the auth tier fetching OIDC paths against private IP space. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail empty — no web-egress equivalent for a self-hosted Node app in those feeds. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/@better-auth/sso/CVE-2026-53513/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/sso
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately configured on-prem/internal IdP where the OIDC endpoints genuinely live on RFC1918 addresses (internal SSO)
  • Service-mesh/sidecar architectures where the app reaches an internal OIDC proxy at 127.0.0.1 or a cluster IP
  • Internal integration testing/staging registering a mock OIDC provider on a private host
  • Cloud metadata probes (169.254.169.254) from unrelated legitimate SDK calls sharing the proxy
Suppression filter
| where DstIpAddr != "127.0.0.1" and not (ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "169.254.169.254/32") and isempty(SrcHostname))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ssoProvider row(s) created/updated around the fetch and inspect oidcConfig.userInfoEndpoint/tokenEndpoint/jwksEndpoint — internal IPs, 127.0.0.1, or 169.254.169.254 confirm SSRF; note the authenticated session that called /sso/register. 2) Contain: delete/disable the malicious ssoProvider entries, block that session/user, and upgrade better-auth to >=1.6.11 (adds the public-routable host allowlist). 3) Hunt: review what the server-side fetch returned (reflected into user profile = non-blind SSRF) for cloud-metadata credentials or internal service data; check whether stolen metadata creds were then used against your cloud control plane.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(DstIpAddr)
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) or ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "127.0.0.0/8") or ipv4_is_in_range(DstIpAddr, "169.254.0.0/16")
| where Url has_any ("/.well-known/openid-configuration","userinfo","jwks","/token","oauth")   // OIDC fetch shapes reachable via a forged provider config
| summarize Fetches = count(), Paths = make_set(Url), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| order by Fetches desc

Better Auth OIDC discovery probe followed by token/registration endpoint access (CVE-2026-53512/53513 recon) AIReconnaissance Low
Correlates a source that requests the OIDC discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration) and then, within 30 minutes, hits a sensitive Better Auth endpoint (/api/auth/oauth2/token, /api/auth/mcp/token, or /sso/register). Aims to catch pre-exploitation fingerprinting of grant types and endpoints preceding refresh-token replay or SSRF registration. Rationale: Chains the discovery-document probe to sensitive endpoint access from the same source within a tight window, reducing the enormous baseline noise of standalone /.well-known/openid-configuration requests. Explicitly low-confidence/hunting because the article body does not describe recon and the discovery doc is legitimately fetched by every SSO integration. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/npm/better-auth/CVE-2026-53512/ • https://better-auth.com/docs/plugins/oidc-provider
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Every legitimate relying-party/SSO client fetches /.well-known/openid-configuration then calls /token as normal OAuth flow — this is the dominant FP
  • OIDC library cold-starts that refresh the discovery cache then immediately exchange tokens
  • Uptime/synthetic monitors polling discovery and token endpoints in sequence
  • Mobile SDKs that re-read discovery on app launch before refresh
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine whether the SrcIp maps to a known registered relying party/client_id; a legitimate client will resolve cleanly, an unknown/external IP walking multiple endpoints will not. 2) Contain: if the source is unrecognised and followed the probe with a 200 on /token or a /sso/register POST, treat as UC1/UC2 and revoke the client's refresh chain / delete the ssoProvider row. 3) Hunt: pivot the SrcIp across UC1 (refresh replay) and UC2 (SSRF egress to private IPs) to confirm whether recon converted to exploitation.
let Window = 30m;
let Probes = ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where Url has "/.well-known/openid-configuration"
    | project ProbeTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ProbeUrl = Url;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has_any ("/api/auth/oauth2/token","/api/auth/mcp/token","/sso/register")
| join kind=inner Probes on SrcIpAddr
| where TimeGenerated between (ProbeTime .. ProbeTime + Window)
| project ProbeTime, AccessTime = TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, ProbeUrl, TargetUrl = Url, HttpMethod, HttpStatusCode
| order by AccessTime desc

UAT-7810 targeted n-day CVE exposure on internet-facing Ruckus/ASUS edge devices AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces managed devices carrying the exact Ruckus and ASUS AiCloud router CVEs UAT-7810 exploits for initial access (CVE-2020-22653, CVE-2020-22658, CVE-2023-25717, CVE-2025-2492), prioritising internet-facing assets. This is an attack-surface hunt tied to the specific n-days named in the Talos campaign, not a generic vuln report. Rationale: Uses the four CVE IDs Talos explicitly attributes to UAT-7810's initial access against Ruckus and ASUS AiCloud routers; scoping to IsInternetFacing devices makes exposure high-fidelity for surface reduction. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/orb-networks-hide-china-espionage
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately vulnerable-but-segmented lab/test routers flagged as internet-facing by NAT misclassification
  • Devices already scheduled for patching in the current maintenance window
  • Vendor virtual appliances that share a CPE string with the affected Ruckus/ASUS models
  • Decommissioned edge devices still reporting inventory before removal
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the device is genuinely internet-reachable on its management/AiCloud service and record firmware version vs the fixed build for each CVE. Step 2 (contain): Restrict management-plane exposure (ACL/VPN-only) and schedule emergency firmware update; where patching is blocked, disable AiCloud/remote admin. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC4 to check whether the device has beaconed to the ORB relay IPs, and inspect the router for unexpected listening ports and web-root scripts (DOGLEASH).

Web server spawning shell/listener on Linux edge host (DOGLEASH web-shell deployment) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts a web server or PHP process spawning an interactive shell, netcat, or interpreter on Linux/IoT hosts — the execution chain Talos describes for DOGLEASH, a lightweight Linux backdoor 'deployed via web shell scripts' that opens a listening TCP port. Targets the router/Linux appliance execution surface, not generic Office macro chains. Rationale: Anchors on Talos's specific description of DOGLEASH being 'deployed via web shell scripts' with 'shell command execution' and opening a listening TCP port; a web-server parent spawning shell/nc on Linux edge devices is the article's execution fingerprint. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • PHP/CGI applications that legitimately shell out to sh for image processing or backups
  • Monitoring agents (Nagios/Zabbix) invoking check scripts under the web user
  • CI/CD or webhook handlers spawning python/perl build steps
  • Cron-invoked maintenance scripts parented to a lingering php-fpm worker
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp/","-e /bin/sh","-e /bin/bash","bash -i","nc -l","ncat -l","socket","pty.spawn")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the child command line — decode any base64, look for reverse-shell (/dev/tcp, nc -l, -e /bin/sh) or listener setup, and identify the writing process's web root. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host from egress, kill the listener, and preserve the web-accessible directory for the dropped web-shell script. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate listening TCP ports on the device (UC covers the hardcoded-password listener), sweep for the UAT-7810 file hashes (UC3), and check for outbound relay to the ORB IPs (UC4).

UAT-7810 LONGLEASH/DOGLEASH malware sample hash on endpoint AIInstallation Medium
Alerts on any file or process matching the SHA256 hashes Talos published for the UAT-7810 toolset (LONGLEASH, DOGLEASH, JARLEASH, LEASHTEST). Direct IOC match against the campaign's confirmed samples. Rationale: Direct SHA256 IOC match against the six hashes Talos attributes to the UAT-7810 toolset; exact-hash matches are the highest-fidelity signal available for this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/orb-networks-hide-china-espionage
ATT&CKT1105 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst or sandbox host intentionally holding the sample for research
  • EDR/AV quarantine copy of the sample generating a secondary file event
  • Threat-intel platform caching the binary during automated enrichment
  • Backup/imaging job re-reading a previously infected volume
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","malware","reverse","detonation"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the hash and identify the host, the writing process, and file path; determine if the host is a sanctioned analysis/sandbox machine. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the endpoint, block the hash org-wide, and preserve the binary for reverse engineering. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to the same host's network events for ORB relay IP contact (UC4), enumerate listening ports for the hardcoded-password backdoor, and hash-sweep the fleet for the remaining toolset samples.

UAT-7810 ORB relay node communication (LONGLEASH C2 infrastructure IPs) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any inbound or outbound traffic to the four UAT-7810 ORB relay/C2 IPs published by Talos, which LONGLEASH uses for multi-protocol proxying and intermediate-C2 forwarding. Direct network IOC match against the campaign's confirmed relay infrastructure. Rationale: Direct match on the four ORB relay/C2 IPs Talos ties to UAT-7810/LONGLEASH; any internal host or edge device contacting these addresses is a high-confidence relay-node or C2 indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/chinese-hackers-develop-longleash-malware-to-expand-orb-network/ • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/orb-networks-hide-china-espionage
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1090.001 T1572 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security appliance actively scanning/validating the IPs against a blocklist
  • Threat-intel enrichment platform test-connecting to the indicator
  • Shared-hosting IP reassigned to a benign service after Talos publication
  • Researcher sandbox detonating the sample and reaching the live C2
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the internal host/edge device and the process/interface generating the traffic, and the protocol/port (watch for DNS/ICMP/SOCKS tunneling and TLS with self-signed PKI). Step 2 (contain): Block the four IPs at the perimeter, isolate the source device, and capture full-packet or netflow for the session. Step 3 (hunt): Determine whether the device is an ingress relay (inbound from the IPs) or egress node, sweep the fleet for the toolset hashes (UC3), and check the same host for the web-shell execution chain (UC2) and unauthorized listening ports.

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-22653", "CVE-2020-22658", "CVE-2023-25717", "CVE-2025-2492")

| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2020-22653", "CVE-2020-22658", "CVE-2023-25717", "CVE-2025-2492")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1") or SHA1 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1") or MD5 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1") or SHA1 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1") or MD5 in~ ("1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1b5649b479fd625de5c8120873644b5eb669cc89cd504582c18e0ae350fd8823", "755fcee1337a252203002ecfdf673a08cfadeda8d738bef2d518a08e0626aa4f", "324d95024fc8da5c92b5a1f4825aed5a2a91c9ca8fb6aa52abb332a4c9cf4257", "bafba443170e54ef7fd431ce7f1b5e202719f3fd022e4ef70788904f574d2cdf", "e799d72929d7ccc7f6b6109742b8cc482838303207efc989543b6e1ca6d16e9c", "3b89d183eb014e29d9d0d4e45fc2b784a7fcfcf31dd48fd3bde30f8d956383d1"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Critical

RedWing MaaS Packages Android Bank Fraud as a Telegram Rental Service

The Hacker News
2026-07-07 11 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A new Android malware operation called RedWing is being rented out on Telegram as a ready-made bank-fraud service. It lets even low-skill criminals take over a victim's phone, steal their banking logins, and capture the one-time codes that protect their accounts. Zimperium's zLabs, which found the operation, says it looks like a new variant of Oblivion, a $300-a-month rent-a-malware tool

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] RedWing dropper delivery: fake ProtonVPN APK and app-store-lookalike download hosts · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] RedWing Android banking trojan C2 beaconing to named panel domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
RedWing Android banking trojan C2 beaconing to named panel domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts corporate DNS/proxy/EDR-network telemetry for resolution of or connection to RedWing MaaS command-and-control panel hosts (redwing.top, redwingqq.top, krusty-crabs.sbs, and the Cloudflare Workers relay api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev). Any managed or BYOD device — including Android endpoints enrolled in MDE — touching these hosts indicates a live RedWing infection phoning home to receive overlay targets, stream the screen, or exfiltrate SMS/OTP data. Rationale: Uses the four RedWing C2/panel hosts (redwing.top, redwingqq.top, krusty-crabs.sbs, api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev) from Zimperium's zLabs IOC bundle — corroborated against the primary vendor blog, distinct from the THN article text. Named C2 domains are the highest-fidelity anchor available since the kit is reskinned and app-name tracking is unreliable. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/redwing-a-mobile-malware-as-a-service-operation • https://github.com/Zimperium/IOC/tree/master/2026-07-RedWing
ATT&CKT1437.001 T1481
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst detonating a RedWing sample in a corporate malware sandbox that egresses through the same DNS/proxy
  • Automated TI enrichment connector (Anomali/Recorded Future/urlscan) resolving the domains for verification
  • Safe Links / proxy URL-rewrite prefetch resolving a submitted link without user intent
  • DNS sinkhole already redirecting the domain — query is logged but connection is benign
  • Security awareness / red-team exercise seeding the domain internally
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the client device/IP that resolved the C2 host and confirm it is a real user endpoint (especially an enrolled Android/BYOD device) rather than a sandbox or TI scanner; check for repeated/beaconing hits vs a one-off lookup. 2) CONTAIN: Block the four domains at DNS/proxy/firewall, isolate or quarantine the offending device via MDM/EDR, and force a corporate credential + banking-app password reset for the user; check for attacker-set call forwarding (*21*) on the carrier account. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the resolved IPs and on the distribution domains (manyrei.live, wmanyrei.icu, yandex-disk.net, offservers.ru) across the estate, and review the device for a recently sideloaded APK with hidden icon and Accessibility grants.
let C2Hosts = dynamic(["redwing.top","redwingqq.top","krusty-crabs.sbs","api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (C2Hosts)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Hosts = dynamic(["redwing.top","redwingqq.top","krusty-crabs.sbs","api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev"]);
union
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has_any (C2Hosts)
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="DNS", Device=Computer, Client=ClientIP, Indicator=Name),
(CommonSecurityLog
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DestinationHostName has_any (C2Hosts) or RequestURL has_any (C2Hosts)
 | project TimeGenerated, Source="Proxy/FW", Device=SourceHostName, Client=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL))
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RedWing dropper delivery: fake ProtonVPN APK and app-store-lookalike download hosts AIDelivery High
Hunts web/proxy/DNS/EDR-network telemetry for contact with the RedWing distribution infrastructure that serves the sideloaded dropper — the fake Proton_VPN.apk on manyrei.live plus the lookalike/typosquat delivery hosts wmanyrei.icu, yandex-disk.net (impersonating Yandex Disk) and offservers.ru. A corporate or managed device fetching an .apk from these hosts marks the initial-access sideload stage before Accessibility abuse and overlay injection begin. Rationale: Anchored on the RedWing distribution URLs from Zimperium's zLabs IOC bundle — manyrei.live/Proton_VPN.apk (the masqueraded ProtonVPN dropper) plus wmanyrei.icu, the Yandex-Disk typosquat yandex-disk.net, and offservers.ru — corroborated by the vendor blog. The literal 'Proton_VPN.apk' filename and the specific hosts are article-specific delivery-stage indicators, and an .apk fetch on a corporate egress is inherently anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://zimperium.com/blog/redwing-a-mobile-malware-as-a-service-operation • https://github.com/Zimperium/IOC/tree/master/2026-07-RedWing
ATT&CKT1660 T1655
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User genuinely searching for Yandex Disk and mistyping to the yandex-disk.net typosquat (visit is still suspicious but not the trojan)
  • Malware analyst/red team downloading the sample for testing through corporate egress
  • URL sandbox/detonation service (proxy DLP, Safe Links) fetching the .apk to scan it
  • Threat-intel connector resolving the distribution domains for enrichment
  • Proxy content-inspection prefetch touching the host without a real user click
Suppression filter
// Sentinel: drop known detonation/scanner egress and require a real client
| where Client !in ("<proxy_sandbox_ip>") // remove line or keep as-is if no sandbox egress IP; alternatively exclude by device
| where Device !has "sandbox" and Device !has "malware-lab"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm whether the request actually retrieved an .apk (check HTTP method/response size and user-agent) and whether the client is a user endpoint versus a scanner; identify the referring phishing/fake-store URL from proxy logs. 2) CONTAIN: Block the distribution domains and the Proton_VPN.apk path at proxy/DNS/firewall, and if an Android device fetched it, isolate via MDM and block sideloading + the default-SMS/Accessibility roles for the app. 3) HUNT: Pivot the client to the C2 detection (redwing.top / redwingqq.top / krusty-crabs.sbs / api-sync-service.mdkd1184.workers.dev) to confirm post-install beaconing, and sweep EmailUrlInfo/proxy for other recipients of the same lure link.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.

DeviceProcessEvents

SecurityEvent

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/

    - attack.execution

            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'

level: high

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
